The reference derives `'wheel-speed'` the same way, as `np.abs` of the velocity that `SessionLoader` returns.\n\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *wheel_speed*?\n\ni. Three steps. The wheel is recorded only when it moves, so `SessionLoader` first interpolates the position onto an even 1000 Hz grid and differentiates it into a velocity, applying a 20 Hz Butterworth low pass while doing so; the speed is the absolute value of that velocity, in radians per second. That trace is then resampled onto the 100 bin centres of each trial. Finally it is cut into three classes at the 33rd and 67th percentile of the session, so the three classes are equally sized within a session.\n\nii. What `SessionLoader.load_wheel` does internally:\n```python\nself.wheel['position'], self.wheel['times'] = interpolate_position(\n    wheel_raw['timestamps'], wheel_raw['position'], freq=fs)\nself.wheel['velocity'], self.wheel['acceleration'] = velocity_filtered(\n    self.wheel['position'], fs=fs, corner_frequency=corner_frequency, order=order)\n```\n\nResampling onto the bin centres, then splitting into three:\n```python\ntraces.append(np.interp(onset + TIME, times[first:last], values[first:last]))\n```\n\n```python\nSPLIT = [100 / 3, 2 * 100 / 3]       # equal sized classes, from percentiles of each session's own trace\n\ndef discretize(trace):\n    \"\"\"Equal sized classes, split at percentiles of this session's own trace.\"\"\"\n    return np.digitize(trace, np.percentile(trace, SPLIT))\n```\n\niii. The interpolation and the filter are not choices, they are what the IBL documentation recommends for computing wheel velocity and what `SessionLoader` does by default, so the reference and this conversion get the same trace.\n\n## 7-d. load_session_spikes(one, eid, pids, pnames):\n    \"\"\"Load and merge the spike sorting of every probe of a session.\n\n    Mirrors `ibl_data_utils.prepare_data`: each probe is loaded with\n A trial is rejected if its window\n    intersects such a gap, or starts before the first / ends after the last spike.\n\n    Args:\n        all_spike_times: (n,) pooled spike times of every cluster, the 100 trial bins, per trial.\n\n    Faithful re-implementation of `ibl_data_utils.get_behavior_per_interval`:\n      * the trace is sliced to the open interval (t_beg, t_end),\n      * a trial is A single global threshold would map whole\n    sessions into one class; per-session tertiles give ~1/3 of samples per class in every\n    session, so chance is a well-defined 1/3 and the shared decoder sees a comparable\n    target in every session.\n\n    Returns (labels (int) in {0,1,2}, thresholds (2,)).\n    \"\"\"\n    finite = values[np.isfinite(values)]\n    thresholds = np.quantile(finite, [1. / 3., 2. / 3.])\n    labels = np.searchsorted(thresholds, values, side='right').astype(np.int64)\n    return labels, thresholds\n\n\ndef trial_number_in_block(probability_left):\n    \"\"\"0-based index of each trial within its block of constant `probabilityLeft`.\n\n    Computed on the *complete* trials table before any trial is excluded, so that the\n    numbering reflects the block structure the mouse actually experienced (the IBL task has\n    an initial 90-trial unbiased block at pLeft = 0.5, then blocks of 20-100 trials\n    alternating between pLeft = 0.8 and 0.2).\n    \"\"\"\n    p = np.asarray(probability_left, dtype=float)\n    new_block = np.ones(len(p), dtype=bool)\n    if len(p) > 1:\n        # NaN != NaN, so a NaN pLeft always starts a new block; those trials are excluded\n        # later by the trials mask anyway.\n        new_block[1:] = ~(p[1:] == p[:-1])\n    block_id = np.cumsum(new_block) - 1\n    # index within block = running count restarting at each block boundary\n    starts = np.nonzero(new_block)[0]\n    within = np.arange(len(p)) - starts[block_id]\n    return within.astype(np.float32), block_id\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Per-session conversion\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\ndef convert_session(eid, verbose=True, collect_debug=False):\n    \"\"\"Convert one session. Returns a dict, or raises on failure.\"\"\"\n    timing = {}\n    one = get_one()\n    brain_regions = get_brain_regions()\n\n    t = time.time()\n    pids, pnames = one.eid2pid(eid)\n    timing['eid2pid'] = time.time() - t\n\n    # ---- neural -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    t = time.time()\n    spikes, clusters = load_session_spikes(one, eid, pids, pnames)\n    timing['load_spikes'] = time.time() - t\n    n_clusters_all = len(clusters)\n\n    t = time.time()\n    keep_idx, beryl_keep = select_neurons(clusters, brain_regions)\n    n_neurons = len(keep_idx)\n    if n_neurons < MIN_NEURONS:\n        raise RuntimeError(f'only {n_neurons} well-isolated grey-matter neurons '\n                           f'(< {MIN_NEURONS})')\n    all_spike_times = spikes['times']       # pooled, unfiltered: used for the data-gap test\n    remap = np.full(n_clusters_all, -1, dtype=np.int64)\n    remap[keep_idx] = np.arange(n_neurons)\n    sc = remap[spikes['clusters']]\n    sel = sc >= 0\n    spike_times = np.ascontiguousarray(spikes['times'][sel])\n    spike_clusters = np.ascontiguousarray(sc[sel])\n    timing['select_neurons'] = time.time() - t\n\n    # ---- trials -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    t = time.time()\n    sess_loader = SessionLoader(one=one, eid=eid)\n    # `load_trials_and_mask` builds the data paper's trial exclusion mask. Note the\n    # reference calls `SessionLoader(one, eid)` positionally, which ibllib 4.0.1 no longer\n    # accepts, hence passing an explicit `sess_loader`.\n    trials, mask = load_trials_and_mask(\n        one=one, eid=eid, max_trial_len=MAX_TRIAL_LEN, sess_loader=sess_loader)\n    mask = np.asarray(mask, dtype=bool)\n    timing['load_trials'] = time.time() - t\n    n_trials_all = len(trials)\n\n    align_times = trials[ALIGN_TIME].to_numpy()\n    in_block, _ = trial_number_in_block(trials['probabilityLeft'].to_numpy())\n\n    # ---- behaviour --------------------------------------------------------------\n    t = time.time()\n    beh_traces, camera_used = load_dynamic_behaviour(sess_loader)\n    timing['load_behaviour'] = time.time() - t\n\n    t = time.time()\n    wheel_vals, wheel_ok = bin_behaviour_per_trial(*beh_traces['wheel-speed'], align_times)\n    me_vals, me_ok = bin_behaviour_per_trial(*beh_traces['whisker-motion-energy'], align_times)\n    timing['bin_behaviour'] = time.time() - t\n\n    # ---- trial selection ---------------------------------------------------------\n    # Mirrors `align_spike_behavior`: keep trials that pass the trials mask AND for which\n    # every behavioural trace could be extracted; additionally require that the neural\n    # recording actually covers the trial window.\n    has_neural = neural_data_available(all_spike_times, align_times)\n    keep_trials = mask & wheel_ok & me_ok & has_neural\n    n_keep = int(keep_trials.sum())\n    if n_keep < MIN_TRIALS:\n        raise RuntimeError(f'only {n_keep} usable trials')\n\n    # ---- bin spikes (only for the trials we keep) --------------------------------\n    t = time.time()\n    binned = bin_spiking_data_fast(spike_times, spike_clusters, n_neurons,\n                                   align_times[keep_trials])\n    timing['bin_spikes'] = time.time() - t\n\n    # ---- inputs ------------------------------------------------------------------\n    tr = trials[keep_trials]\n    inp = np.empty((n_keep, 2, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n    inp[:, 0, :] = BIN_CENTRES.astype(np.float32)\n    inp[:, 1, :] = in_block[keep_trials][:, None]\n\n    # ---- outputs -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    # choice: IBL codes +1 / -1. Verified empirically (see CONVERSION_NOTES Step 4):\n    # on correct trials with the stimulus on the left, choice == +1; on correct trials with\n    # the stimulus on the right, choice == -1. So +1 is a leftward choice.\n    choice = tr['choice'].to_numpy()\n    choice_out = (choice < 0).astype(np.int64)          # left -> 0, right -> 1\n\n    pleft = tr['probabilityLeft'].to_numpy()\n    prior_out = np.full(n_keep, -1, dtype=np.int64)\n    for value, code in ((0.2, 0), (0.5, 1), (0.8, 2)):\n        prior_out[np.isclose(pleft, value)] = code\n    if np.any(prior_out < 0):\n        bad = np.unique(pleft[prior_out < 0])\n        raise RuntimeError(f'unexpected probabilityLeft values {bad}')\n\n    wheel_kept = wheel_vals[keep_trials]\n    me_kept = me_vals[keep_trials]\n    wheel_lab, wheel_thr = discretize_tertiles(wheel_kept)\n    me_lab, me_thr = discretize_tertiles(me_kept)\n\n    out = np.empty((n_keep, 4, NBINS), dtype=np.int64)\n    out[:, 0, :] = choice_out[:, None]\n    out[:, 1, :] = prior_out[:, None]\n    out[:, 2, :] = wheel_lab\n    out[:, 3, :] = me_lab\n\n    result = dict(\n        eid=str(eid),\n        neural=binned,                      # uint8 (n_keep, n_neurons, NBINS)\n        input=inp,\n        output=out,\n        beryl=beryl_keep,\n        n_clusters_all=int(n_clusters_all),\n        n_good_all=int((clusters['label'].to_numpy() >= QC_LABEL).sum()),\n        n_neurons=int(n_neurons),\n        n_probes=len(pids),\n        n_trials_all=int(n_trials_all),\n        n_trials_mask=int(mask.sum()),\n        n_trials_no_neural=int((mask & ~has_neural).sum()),\n        n_trials_no_behaviour=int((mask & has_neural & ~(wheel_ok & me_ok)).sum()),\n        n_trials_kept=n_keep,\n        camera_used=camera_used,\n        wheel_thresholds=wheel_thr,\n        me_thresholds=me_thr,\n        frac_correct=float((trials['feedbackType'].to_numpy() == 1).mean()),\n        timing=timing,\n    )\n    if collect_debug:\n        result['debug'] = dict(\n            trials=trials, mask=mask, keep_trials=keep_trials,\n            align_times=align_times, in_block=in_block,\n            wheel_trace=beh_traces['wheel-speed'], me_trace=beh_traces['whisker-motion-energy'],\n            wheel_vals=wheel_kept, me_vals=me_kept,\n            spike_times=spike_times, spike_clusters=spike_clusters,\n        )\n    if verbose:\n        print(f'  [{eid}] probes={len(pids)} clusters={n_clusters_all} '\n              f'good={result[\"n_good_all\"]} kept_neurons={n_neurons} '\n              f'trials={n_trials_all}->mask {int(mask.sum())}'\n              f'->(-{int((mask & ~has_neural).sum())} no-ephys, '\n              f'-{int((mask & has_neural & ~(wheel_ok & me_ok)).sum())} no-behaviour)'\n              f'->kept {n_keep} '\n              f'camera={camera_used} '\n              f'({sum(timing.values()):.1f}s)', flush=True)\n    return result\n\n\ndef _worker(eid):\n    try:\n        return convert_session(eid, verbose=True)\n    except Exception as exc:       # noqa: BLE001 -- one bad session must not kill the run\n        return {'eid': str(eid), 'error': f'{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}',\n                'traceback': traceback.format_exc()}\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Diagnostic plots\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\ndef plot_processing(res, outpath):\n    \"\"\"Plot every processing step for one session, to verify alignment/discretization.\"\"\"\n    import matplotlib\n    matplotlib.use('Agg')\n    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n\n    dbg = res['debug']\n    trials, keep = dbg['trials'], dbg['keep_trials']\n    align = dbg['align_times'][keep]\n    neural = res['neural'].astype(np.float32)\n    inp, out = res['input'], res['output']\n    n_keep = neural.shape[0]\n    tr_edges = BIN_RIGHT_EDGES\n    tr_ctr = BIN_CENTRES\n\n    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(26, 30))\n    gs = fig.add_gridspec(7, 3, hspace=0.45, wspace=0.22)\n\n    # --- 1. population PSTH: must show a stimulus-locked transient at t = 0 -----------\n    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :])\n    psth = neural.mean(axis=(0, 1)) / BINSIZE\n    ax.plot(tr_ctr, psth, lw=2)\n    ax.axvline(0, color='r', ls='--', label='stimulus onset')\n    ax.set_xlabel('time from stimulus onset (s)')\n    ax.set_ylabel('mean firing rate (sp/s)')\n    ax.set_title(f'{res[\"eid\"]}: population PSTH aligned to {ALIGN_TIME} '\n                 f'({res[\"n_neurons\"]} neurons, {n_keep} trials)')\n    ax.legend()\n\n    # --- 2. single-trial raster reconstructed from raw spike times vs binned matrix ----\n    k = min(3, n_keep - 1)\n    t0 = sc[sel], '|', ms=2, color='k')\n    ax.axvline(0, color='r', ls='--')\n    ax.set_xlim(TIME_WINDOW)\n    ax.set_title(f'raw spike raster, trial {k}')\n    ax.set_xlabel('time from stim onset (s)'); ax.set_ylabel('neuron')\n\n    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1])\n    ax.imshow(neural[k], aspect='auto', interpolation='nearest', origin='lower',\n              extent=[TIME_WINDOW[0], TIME_WINDOW[1], ax.set_ylabel('neuron')\n\n    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2])\n    # per-bin totals from the two routes must agree exactly\n    hist = np.zeros(NBINS)\n    b = np.floor((st[sel] - (t0 + TIME_WINDOW[0])) / BINSIZE).astype(int)\n    b = b[(b >= 0) & (b < NBINS)]\n    np.add.at(hist, b, 1)\n    ax.step(tr_ctr, hist, where='mid', label='from raw spike times')\n    ax.step(tr_ctr, neural[k].sum(axis=0), where='mid', ls='--', label='from binned matrix')\n    ax.legend(); ax.set_title('per-bin spike totals agree')\n    ax.set_xlabel('time from stim onset (s)')\n\n    # --- 3. ax.plot(wt[win] - t0, wv[win], color='0.6', lw=1, label='raw |wheel velocity| (~1 kHz)')\n    ax.plot(tr_edges, dbg['wheel_vals'][k], 'o-', ms=3, color='C0',\n            label='resampled onto bin right edges')\n    for thr in res['wheel_thresholds']:\n        ax.axhline(thr, color='C3', ls=':', lw=1)\n    ax.axvline(0, color='r', ls='--')\n    ax.set_yscale('log')\n    ax.set_title(f'wheel ax.legend()\n\n    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[3, 0])\n    ax.step(tr_edges, out[k, 2], where='post', color='C0')\n    ax.set_title('discretized wheel speed (trial %d)' % k)\n# Dataset Conversion Notes\n\n## Overview\n- **Dataset**: IBL Brain Wide Map (BWM) public release, served from a local ONE cache at `/app/data/one_cache`\n- **Reference papers**: IBL et al. 2025 *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour* (Nature) = \"datapaper\"; Zhang et al. 2026 *Exploiting correlations across trials and behavioral sessions to improve neural decoding* (Neuron) = \"methodpaper\"\n- **Reference code**: `/app/code/code_zhang2025` (Zhang et al. caching + decoding pipeline)\n- **Date started**: 2026-09-20\n- **Goal**: Convert to decoder-compatible format (`/app/converted_data.pkl`)\n\n## Step 0: Setup and Initialization\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nDirectory contents of `/app`:\n- `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` (this file)\n- `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yaml`, `stage_cache.sh`, `.manifest` — container/env plumbing\n- `code/` — `code_zhang2025` (method-paper code) and `ibllib` (library source copy)\n- `data/one_cache/` — the ONE cache (release tables + symlinked lab/Subjects trees)\n- `datapaper.pdf`, `methodpaper.pdf`, `dataarchitecture.pdf`, `methods.txt` — references\n- `ibl_docs/` — downloaded ONE/ibllib/iblatlas documentation\n- `decoder.py`, `train_decoder.py` — provided decoder + validation harness\n\nEnvironment check: `python3` works; `numpy 2.3.5`, `torch 2.6.0+cu124`, `ONE-api 3.5.2`,\n`ibllib 4.0.1`, `iblatlas 1.2.0` all import. Hardware: 128 CPUs, 1006 GB RAM, 3.4 TB disk,\n1x NVIDIA L4 (23 GB).\n\n**ONE access**: the cache is used offline through cached Alyx REST responses\n(`/app/data/one_cache/.rest`) plus an auth token staged into `$HOME/.one`. The working\nrecipe is\n\n```python\none = ONE(base_url='https://openalyx.internationalbrainlab.org',\n          silent=True, cache_dir='/app/data/one_cache')   # -> mode='remote'\n```\n\nUsing `mode='local'` + `one.load_cache(tag='Brainwidemap')` does **not** work: that\nrelease table was built 2025-02-20 and lists `alf/_ibl_trials.table.pqt`, whereas the\nstaged files live under the newer revision folder `alf/#2025-03-03#/`. With the local\ntable, `SessionLoader.load_trials()` silently returns a 1-column frame\n(`goCueTrigger_times` only). In `remote` mode (served from the `.rest` cache) all 20\ntrial columns load correctly. This was verified explicitly before writing any conversion\ncode.\n\n---\n\n## Step 1: Reference Code Exploration\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nReference pipeline entry point: `/app/code/code_zhang2025/src/0_data_caching.py`.\nIt sets\n\n```python\nparams = {'interval_len': 2, 'binsize': 0.02, 'single_region': False,\n          'align_time': 'stimOn_times', 'time_window': (-.5, 1.5)}\nbeh_names = ['choice', 'reward', 'block', 'wheel-speed', 'whisker-motion-energy']\n```\n\nand then calls, in order: `prepare_data` → `list_brain_regions` → `select_brain_regions`\n→ `bin_spiking_data` → `bin_behaviors` → `align_spike_behavior`.\n\n### Key Functions Identified\n| Function | File | Stage | Purpose |\n|----------|------|-------|---------|\n| `prepare_data` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | LOADING | `one.eid2pid(eid)`; loads each probe with `load_spiking_data`; `merge_probes`; `load_trials_and_mask(max_trial_len=10.0)`; `load_anytime_behaviors` |\n| `load_spiking_data` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | LOADING/CURATION | `SpikeSortingLoader.load_spike_sorting()` + `merge_clusters(...).to_df()`. `qc=None` (default) keeps every cluster; `qc=1` keeps `label >= 1` (\"good\"/well-isolated) |\n| `merge_probes` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | LOADING | concatenates probes of one session into a single cluster/spike set, re-indexing `spikes['clusters']`, re-sorting spikes by time |\n| `load_trials_and_mask` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | CURATION | `SessionLoader.load_trials()`; builds a boolean mask excluding RT<0.08 s, RT>2 s, `feedback_times-goCue_times > max_trial_len`, NaN in {stimOn_times, choice, feedback_times, probabilityLeft, firstMovement_times, feedbackType}, and `choice == 0` |\n| `list_brain_regions` / `select_brain_regions` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | PROCESSING | `BrainRegions().acronym2acronym(..., mapping='Beryl')`; with `single_region=False` returns one group with **all** Beryl regions |\n| `bin_spiking_data` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | PROCESSING | intervals = `stimOn_times + (-0.5, 1.5)`; per-trial `bincount2D(times, clusters, xbin=0.02, xlim=[t_beg,t_end])`, truncated to `n_bins = ceil(2/0.02) = 100` |\n| `get_spike_data_per_interval` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | PROCESSING | the per-trial worker for the above (multiprocessing) |\n| `load_target_behavior` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | LOADING | `SessionLoader.load_wheel()` → `wheel-speed = abs(velocity)`; `SessionLoader.load_motion_energy(views=['left'/'right'])` → `whiskerMotionEnergy` |\n| `get_behavior_per_interval` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | PROCESSING | slices the behavioural trace to the trial interval and `interp1d`-resamples onto `np.linspace(beg+binsize, end, n_bins)` (i.e. the **right edge of each 20 ms bin**); marks the interval bad if the trace starts >1 bin late or ends >1 bin early, if the interval time is NaN, or (when `allow_nans=False`) if it contains NaNs |\n| `bin_behaviors` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | PROCESSING | builds `choice`, `block` (=`probabilityLeft`), `reward` (=`rewardVolume>1`), `contrast` per trial, plus the interpolated dynamic traces; called with `allow_nans=True` |\n| `align_spike_behavior` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | CURATION | drops trials where any behaviour is `None` **and** trials failing `trials_mask` |\n| `standardize_spike_data` | `src/utils/data_loader_utils.py` | PROCESSING | per-time-bin z-scoring; belongs to the *model*, not the dataset (their cached HF dataset stores raw spike counts as `np.ubyte`) |\n\n### Notes\n- The cached dataset the reference writes contains **raw spike counts** per (trial, time-bin,\n  neuron), stored sparsely as unsigned bytes. Standardisation happens at model-fit time.\n  Our target format wants neural activity per trial as `(n_neurons, n_timepoints)`, so we\n  store the same raw spike counts (as `float32`), transposed.\n- `prepare_data` calls `load_spiking_data` **without** `qc`, i.e. it keeps all Kilosort\n  clusters including MUA. The data paper instead uses only well-isolated neurons\n  (`label >= 1`). See Step 4 for how this discrepancy is resolved.\n- `load_spiking_data` also calls `spike_loader.raw_electrophysiology(band=\"ap\", stream=True).fs`\n  purely to record the AP sampling rate in metadata. That streams raw data over the network\n  and is not needed for binning, so it is not reproduced here.\n- The decoding scripts (`1_/2_/3_decode_*.py`, `utils/data_loader_utils.py`) show how the\n  cached data is consumed: `choice` as a classification target, `wheel-speed` /\n  `whisker-motion-energy` as **time-varying** (length-T) regression targets, `block`/prior\n  per trial. `MultiRegionDataModule.list_regions` excludes `root` and `void`.\n\n---\n\n## Step 2: Dataset Exploration\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Data Structure\n`/app/data/one_cache/` is a standard ONE also what the task specification requires.\n2. **Spike counts, unnormalised.** The reference caches raw counts (`np.ubyte`) and\n   z-scores only inside the model (`standardize_spike_data`). `train_decoder.py` does its\n   own SVD-based projection, so raw counts are the right thing to store.\n3. **Neuron QC: `label >= 1` + grey matter.** See Step 4. Use the exact step names below when documenting progress in CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n**STATUS TRACKING**: At the start of each step, update its status to `IN PROGRESS` in CONVERSION_NOTES.md. When complete, update to `COMPLETE`. This helps you and the user track progress.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 0: Setup and Initialization\\n\\n**Goal**: Set up the working environment and create the notes file.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. **FIRST**: Create `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` with the template structure shown at the end of this document\\n2. Do NOT look outside this project directory.\\n\\n**Goal**: Understand the native data structure\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Identify how data is organized (all files, formats, hierarchies)\\n- Determine available variables and their meanings\\n- Check data dimensions and data types\\n- Look for documentation or README files\\n- Note the data organization and structure\\n- Note dataset size parameters such as the **total number** of subjects (mice), sessions, trials, and neurons\\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented the data structure, file formats, size, and available variables in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 2\\\".\\n\\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 3, update Step 2 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 3: Reference Text Reading\\n\\n**Goal**: Extract key information from the paper and methods.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Scan the reference papers and methods.txt for important details about the data\\n- Look for and note to file:\\n  - Any information about dataset size (number of neurons, subjects, sessions, trials)\\n  - Fraction of data with different values, e.g. fraction of rewarded outcomes\\n  - Data processing, curation, and filtering\\n  - Variables important to experiments\\n  - Temporal alignment\\n  - Temporal binning\\n- Read the reference paper to find information about expected decoder accuracy.\\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented expected dataset statistics and processing details in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 3\\\".\\n\\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 4, update Step 3 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 4: Check for Consistency\\n\\n**Goal**: Verify your understanding is consistent across all sources. \\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Compare your understanding of:\\n  - Important functions from exploring the reference code\\n  - Dataset structure from exploring the dataset\\n  - Analysis described in the reference texts\\n- Note and investigate any discrepancies\\n- In particular, look for discrepancies in:\\n  - Experimental and behavioral variables\\n  - Data processing\\n  - Data curation\\n- Iterate until your understanding of the reference code, dataset, and reference texts are consistent\\n\\n**Done when**: You have resolved all discrepancies and documented your final understanding in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 4\\\".\\n\\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 5, update Step 4 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 5: Mapping Planning\\n\\n**Goal**: Create a detailed plan for mapping source data to target format.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Map source data elements to target format components:\\n  - Which variables contain neural activity?\\n  - Identify ALL available experimental variables\\n  - Which variables should be decoder **inputs** vs **outputs**? (Follow Decoder Task section)\\n  - How to discretize continuous outputs (Follow Decoder Task section)\\n  - Which inputs/outputs should be **time-varying** vs **per-trial** (Follow Decoder Task section)\\n  - How does the reference code load and manipulate this data?\\n  - When possible, import or copy code from the reference code in `/app/code` directory. \\n- Consult CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Steps 1-4 and reference materials to determine:\\n  - Temporal binning for spike rates (if applicable)\\n  - Temporal alignment of trials\\n  - Data filtering and curation rules for neurons, trials, and sessions\\n  - Brain regions recorded from\\n- Mapping should be consistent with CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Steps 1-4.\\n- Check for variables indicating valid data periods — exclude invalid data\\n- Note all decisions, edge cases, and data quality issues\\n- Plan and document **sanity and consistency checks** based on dataset size information from the reference texts, code, and data\\n\\n**Done when**:\\n- You have a complete mapping document in CONVERSION_NOTES.md specifying every source-to-target variable mapping under \\\"Step 5\\\"\\n- You have documented all decisions under \\\"Step 5\\\"\\n- You have documented sanity and consistency checks under \\\"Step 5\\\"\\n\\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 6, update Step 5 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 6: Script Development\\n\\n**Goal**: Write the conversion script to `/app/convert_data.py`.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Write all conversion code in the file `/app/convert_data.py`\\n- Script should run as **`python -u /app/convert_data.py <outpicklefile>`**\\n- Include options:\\n  - `--full` (default): Process all sessions\\n  - `--sample`: Process only 2 sessions for testing\\n  - `--show-processing`: Plot visualizations of EVERY processing step for up to 2 sessions. Save plots as `processing_<session_id>.png`.\\n- Reuse code from reference code bases where appropriate\\n- Use the `ONE` API to interface with the data. Do not directly read the data files. \\n- Write efficient code:\\n  - Vectorize loops\\n  - Avoid unnecessary file I/O\\n  - Use parallel processing if beneficial\\n  - Print timing information to find bottlenecks\\n- Plots for `--show-processing` mode should visually convince the user that every step of the conversion is correct.\\n  - There are no temporal misalignments\\n  - Discretization of continuous outputs is correct\\n- Write clear, well-documented functions\\n- Handle missing data appropriately (consult references, use sensible defaults, document)\\n- Validate data shapes and types at each step\\n- Include sanity checks (e.g., trial counts match across arrays)\\n\\n**Done when**: `/app/convert_data.py` exists and runs efficiently without errors.\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 7 until `/app/convert_data.py` exists and you have updated Step 6 in CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\\n\\n**Goal**: Validate the conversion on a small sample before processing the full dataset.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Run `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing 2>&1 | tee /app/conversion_sample_out.txt`\\n  a. Verify the sample data structure matches the specification.\\n  b. Check dimensions are consistent across trials/sessions.\\n  c. Check that no data is missed during conversion. \\n  d. Validate that metadata accurately describes the data.\\n2. Improve efficiency of conversion.\\n  a. Look at and note timing information for the conversion. \\n  b. Estimate how long the full conversion will run. When you do this, make sure that your estimate accounts for differences in lengths/numbers of trials/sessions. \\n  c. If full conversion time estimate is longer than 15 minutes, speed up the code by writing more efficient code (vectorizing loops, removing unnecessary or redundant computations) and/or including parallel processing. \\n3. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/sample_data.pkl --verify-only 2>&1 | tee /app/verification_sample_out.txt`.\\n4. Analyze the output file `/app/verification_sample_out.txt`:\\n  a. Verify no errors reported.\\n  b. Attempt to address any warnings\\n  c. Check input ranges and output value distributions against expectations from reference texts.\\n\\n**Done when**: \\n- `/app/sample_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\\n- `/app/verification_sample_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\\n- Processing plots show no anomalies\\n- Document sample statistics in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 7\\\"\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 8 until `/app/sample_data.pkl` and `/app/verification_sample_out.txt` files exist, and CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 7 is filled in. \\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 8: Sample Decoder Training\\n\\n**Goal**: Verify the decoder runs successfully on sample data.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/sample_data.pkl 2>&1 | tee /app/train_decoder_sample_out.txt`\\n2. **Check training**: Verify loss decreases over epochs\\n3. **Check accuracy**: Verify accuracy is above chance for EVERY output\\n\\n**Investigate any issues**:\\n- If accuracy is low: check for conversion bugs or reconsider output representation\\n\\n**Done when**: \\n- Decoder training completes without errors\\n- Loss decreases over epochs\\n- Accuracies are above chance\\n- Document all results in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 8\\\"\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 9 until `/app/train_decoder_sample_out.txt` file exists, and CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 8 is filled in. \\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 9: Full Conversion and Validation\\n\\n**Goal**: Process the complete dataset.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Review your time estimate from Step 7.\\n2. If estimated time is long (e.g. longer than 15 minutes), optimize bottlenecks first.\\n3. Run `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/converted_data.pkl --full 2>&1 | tee /app/conversion_full_out.txt`\\n4. As the code runs, update your estimates of how long processing will take. If it is much longer than your previous estimate (> 1.5x), kill the process, optimize bottlenecks, and repeat. \\n5. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/converted_data.pkl --verify-only 2>&1 | tee /app/verification_full_out.txt`. \\n6. Check that no data was lost during conversion \\n7. Spot-check a few sessions to verify data integrity\\n8. **Check for consistency** between dataset statistics in `/app/verification_full_out.txt` and the reference texts\\n9. Investigate any inconsistencies, and revise the conversion script until all dataset statistics are consistent\\n\\n**Done when**:\\n- `/app/converted_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\\n- `/app/verification_full_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\\n- **ALL** dataset statistics are consistent with values from reference texts\\n- You have documented statistics and consistency in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 9\\\"\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 10 until `/app/converted_data.pkl` and `/app/verification_full_out.txt` files exist and CONVERSION_NOTES.MD Step 9 is filled in.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 10: Critical Review 1\\n\\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Compare accuracy to expectations based on the papers. \\n\\n**Done when**: \\n1. Full decoder training completes (the script finishes running)\\n2. Accuracy results are documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 11\\\" with a table of accuracies\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 12: Critical Review 2\\n\\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Perform all of the following checks:\\n\\n**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\\n- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\\n- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \\n- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \\n\\n**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to papers**\\n- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference papers\\n- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the papers's accuracy for each variable\\n- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \\n- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \\n\\n**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\\n- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \\n\\n**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\\n1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\\n2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\\n3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\\n4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \\n5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and papers. \\n\\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\\n\\n**Report all checks and results** to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 12\\\".\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\\n\\n**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\\n  - Key decisions and rationale\\n  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\\n  - Validation results and tables\\n  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\\n- Create a user-facing `/app/README.md` summarizing:\\n  - Dataset description\\n  - How to load and use the converted data\\n  - Output format specification\\n  - Key statistics\\n- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `/app/cache/` folder\\n- Create `/app/cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\\n\\n**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\\n\\n**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.\\n22\\t\\n23\\tRecordings\\n24\\t\\n25\\tIn these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. To ensure reproducibility, one brain location was targeted in every mouse in every laboratory, as described elsewhere25. Only sessions with at least 400 trials were retained for further analyses. Data were uploaded to a central server, preprocessed and shared through a standardized interface. To perform spike sorting on the recordings, we used a version of Kilosort with custom additions. This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe. To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.\\n26\\t\\n27\\tMethods\\n28\\t\\n29\\tn brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. After the quiescence period, a visual stimulus (Gabor patch) appeared on either the left or right (±35° azimuth) of the screen, with a contrast randomly sampled from a predefined set (100, 25, 12.5, 6 or 0%). A 100-ms tone (5-kHz sine wave) was played at stimulus onset. Mice had 60 s to move the wheel and make a response. Stimuli were yoked to the rotation of the response wheel, such that a 1-mm movement of the wheel moved the stimulus by 4 visual degrees. A response was registered if the centre of the stimulus crossed the  ±35° azimuth line from its original position. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. If the mouse responded incorrectly or failed to reach either threshold within the 60-s window, a white-noise burst was played for 500 ms and the inter-trial interval was between 1 and 1.5 s. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.\\n30\\t\\n31\\tEach session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Specifically, the 100%, 25%, 12.5% and 6% contrast trials were each presented 10 times on each side, and the 0% contrast was presented 10 times in total (that is, the ratio of the 100, 25, 12.5, 6 and 0% contrasts were set at 2, 2, 2, 2 and 1, respectively). The side (and thus correct movement) for the 0% contrast trials was chosen randomly between the right and left with equal probability. This initial block of 90 trials is referred to as the unbiased block (50:50).\\n32\\t\\n33\\tAfter the unbiased block, trials were presented in biased blocks: in right-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 80% of the trials, whereas in left-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 20% of the trials. The ratio of the contrasts remained as above (2:2:2:2:1). Whether the first biased block in a session was left or right was randomly chosen, and blocks were then alternated. The length of a block was drawn from an exponential distribution with scale parameter of 60 trials, but truncated to lie between 20 and 100 trials.\\n34\\t\\n35\\tThe automated shaping protocol for training involved two collections of sessions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. They also experienced a debiasing protocol, which was intended to dissuade them from persisting with just one of the choices. Once they were performing sufficiently well on all non-zero contrasts, they were faced with the biased blocks. When, in turn, performance on those was adequate (including on 0% contrast trials, which are informed by the block), they graduated to recording. Supplementary Figure 8a shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the first and second collections (these were not correlated). Supplementary Figure 8b shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the second collection and the performance during the recording sessions. These were also not correlated.\\n36\\t\\n37\\tInclusion criteria\\n38\\t\\n39\\tWe applied a set of inclusion criteria to sessions, probes and neurons to ensure data quality. Supplementary Table 1 lists the consequences of these criteria for the number of sessions and probes that passed the criteria.\\n40\\tSessions and insertions\\n41\\t\\n42\\tEach Neuropixels insertion was repeated in at least two laboratories, with reproducibility of outcomes across laboratories verified with extensive analyses that we have previously reported25.\\n43\\t\\n44\\tSessions were included in the data release if the mice performed at least 250 trials, with a performance of at least 90% correct on 100% contrast trials for both left and right blocks, and, to be able to analyse the feedback variable, if there were at least 3 trials with incorrect choices (after applying the trial exclusions below). Furthermore, sessions were included in the release only if they reached threshold on a collection of hardware tests (definitions are available from GiHub (https://int-brain-lab.github.io/iblenv/_autosummary/ibllib.qc.task_metrics.html)).\\n45\\t\\n46\\tInsertions were excluded if the neural data failed the whole recording per visually assessed criteria of the ‘Recording Inclusion metrics and Guidelines for Optimal Reproducibility’ (RIGOR) from ref. 25, by presenting major artefacts (see examples in ref. 28) or if the probe tract could not be recovered during the histology procedure. Furthermore, only insertions for which alignments had been resolved (see appendix 6 of ref. 25 for definitions) were used in this study.\\n47\\t\\n48\\tAfter applying these criteria, a total of 459 sessions, 699 insertions and 621,733 neurons remained, constituting the publicly released dataset.\\n49\\tTrials\\n50\\t\\n51\\tFor the analyses presented here, trials were excluded if one of the following trial events could not be detected: choice, probabilityLeft, feebackType, feeback times, stimON times and firstMovement times. Neurons that passed these criteria were termed well-isolated neurons (or often just ‘neurons’) in this study. Out of the 621,733 units collected, 75,708 were considered well-isolated neurons. Final analyses were additionally restricted to regions that were designated grey matter in the adult mouse Allen Common Coordinate framework6, contained at least five well-isolated neurons per session and were recorded from in at least two such sessions.\\n55\\t\\n56\\tVideo analysis\\n57\\t\\n58\\tWe briefly describe the video analysis pipeline (full details can be found in ref. 105). The recording rigs contained three cameras: one called ‘left’ at full resolution (1,280 × 1,024) and 60 Hz, filming the mouse from one side; one called ‘right’, filming the mouse symmetrically from the other side at half resolution (640 × 512) and 150 Hz; and one called ‘body’ at half resolution and 30 Hz, filming the body of the mouse from above. We developed several quality-control metrics to detect raw video issues such as poor illumination (as infrared light bulbs broke) or accidental misplacement of the cameras105.\\n59\\t\\n60\\tWe computed the motion energy (the mean across pixels of the absolute value of the difference between adjacent frames) of the whisker pad areas in the ‘left’ and ‘right’ videos (Fig. 1d). The whisker pad area was empirically defined using a rectangular bounding box anchored between the nose tip and the eye, both found using DeepLabCut106 (DLC; see more below). This metric quantifies motion in the whisker pad area and has a temporal resolution of the respective camera.\\n61\\t\\n62\\tWe also performed markerless pose estimation of body parts using DLC31, which is used in a fully automated pipeline in IBL (v.2.1) to track various body parts such as the paws, nose, tongue and pupil (Fig. 1d). Furthermore, we developed several quality-control metrics for the DLC traces105.\\n63\\t\\n64\\tOverview of decoding\\n65\\t\\n66\\tWe performed a decoding analysis to measure how much information the activity of populations of neurons contained about task variables such as stimulus side and choice. To do this we, used cross-validated, maximum-likelihood regression with L1 regularization (to zero out the contribution from noisy neurons). The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). These factors are discussed further below and include a variety of behavioural and task variables: stimulus side, choice, feedback and wheel speed and velocity. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions. The P values for all regions were then subjected to FDR correction for multiple comparisons at q = 0.01.\\n67\\t\\n68\\tDecoding target variables\\n69\\t\\n70\\tStimulus side, choice and feedback were treated as binary target variables for logistic regression. For stimulus side, trials that had zero contrast were excluded. We used the LogisticRegression module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 20,000 maximum iterations, “l1” penalty, “liblinear” solver and “fit_intercept” set to True. We balanced decoder classes by weighting samples by the inverse of the class frequency, 1/(2Pi,class). Decoding performance was evaluated using the balanced accuracy of classification, which is the average of the recall probabilities for the two classes. Supplementary Figure 9 shows histograms of the regression coefficients for all the variables.\\n71\\t\\n72\\tWheel values (speed and velocity) change over the course of a trial, unlike the previous decoding targets, and we therefore had to treat these target variables differently. We averaged wheel values in nonoverlapping 20-ms bins, starting 200 ms before first wheel-movement time and ending at 1,000 ms after first wheel-movement time. Spike counts were similarly binned. The target value for a given bin (ending at time t) was decoded from spikes in a preceding (causal) window spanning W bins (ending at times t, …, t-W). Therefore, if decoding from n neurons, there were (W + 1)n predictors of the target variable in a given bin. In practice, we used W = 10. To decode these continuous-valued targets, we performed linear regression using the Lasso module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 1,000 maximum iterations and “fit_intercept” set to True. To do this we, used cross-validated, maximum-likelihood regression with L1 regularization (to zero out the contribution from noisy neurons). The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). These factors are discussed further below and include a variety of behavioural and task variables: stimulus side, choice, feedback and wheel speed and velocity. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions. The P values for all regions were then subjected to FDR correction for multiple comparisons at q = 0.01.\\\\n\\\\nDecoding target variables\\\\n\\\\nStimulus side, choice and feedback were treated as binary target variables for logistic regression. For stimulus side, trials that had zero contrast were excluded. We used the LogisticRegression module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 20,000 maximum iterations, “l1” penalty, “liblinear” solver and “fit_intercept” set to True. We balanced decoder classes by weighting samples by the inverse of the class frequency, 1/(2Pi,class). Decoding performance was evaluated using the balanced accuracy of classification, which is the average of the recall probabilities for the two classes. We averaged wheel values in nonoverlapping 20-ms bins, starting 200 ms before first wheel-movement time and ending at 1,000 ms after first wheel-movement time. Spike counts were similarly binned. The target value for a given bin (ending at time t) was decoded from spikes in a preceding (causal) window spanning W bins (ending at times t, …, t-W). Therefore, if decoding from n neurons, there were (W + 1)n predictors of the target variable in a given bin. In practice, we used W = 10. To decode these continuous-valued targets, we performed linear regression using the Lasso module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 1,000 maximum iterations and “fit_intercept” set to True. For each trial k, neural activity has size N x T, where N is the number of neurons and T the number of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For each trial, we constructed X \\\\in R^{N x T}  by aggregating spike counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate of the true behavior y \\\\in R^P. y is constant within a trial (“per-trial decoding”); when P = T, y varies across time (“per-timestep decoding”).\\n\\nWe apply our models to 433 IBL sessions,17 covering 270 brain regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel speed, and whisker motion energy.\\n\\n In the IBL experiments, mice rotate a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as their choice (Figure 1A). For the first 90 trials, the stimulus appears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subsequent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allowing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior) about stimulus location. Additionally, wheel speed and whisker motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections “data processing” and “hyperparameter selection” for details.\\n\\nData processing\\n\\nIBL trial-aligned dataset\\n\\nFor choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session.\\n\\nIBL trial-unaligned dataset\\n\\nWe focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials, capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials.\\n\\nFrom \\\"A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour\\\"\\n\\nWe trained 139 mice (94 male and 45 female) on the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) decision-making task (Fig. 1a,b). On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.\\n\\nRecordings\\n\\nIn these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. To ensure reproducibility, one brain location was targeted in every mouse in every laboratory, as described elsewhere25. Only sessions with at least 400 trials were retained for further analyses. Data were uploaded to a central server, preprocessed and shared through a standardized interface. To perform spike sorting on the recordings, we used a version of Kilosort with custom additions. This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe. To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.\\n\\nMethods\\n\\nn brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. After the quiescence period, a visual stimulus (Gabor patch) appeared on either the left or right (±35° azimuth) of the screen, with a contrast randomly sampled from a predefined set (100, 25, 12.5, 6 or 0%). A 100-ms tone (5-kHz sine wave) was played at stimulus onset. Mice had 60 s to move the wheel and make a response. Stimuli were yoked to the rotation of the response wheel, such that a 1-mm movement of the wheel moved the stimulus by 4 visual degrees. A response was registered if the centre of the stimulus crossed the  ±35° azimuth line from its original position. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. If the mouse responded incorrectly or failed to reach either threshold within the 60-s window, a white-noise burst was played for 500 ms and the inter-trial interval was between 1 and 1.5 s. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.\\n\\nEach session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Specifically, the 100%, 25%, 12.5% and 6% contrast trials were each presented 10 times on each side, and the 0% contrast was presented 10 times in total (that is, the ratio of the 100, 25, 12.5, 6 and 0% contrasts were set at 2, 2, 2, 2 and 1, respectively). The side (and thus correct movement) for the 0% contrast trials was chosen randomly between the right and left with equal probability. This initial block of 90 trials is referred to as the unbiased block (50:50).\\n\\nAfter the unbiased block, trials were presented in biased blocks: in right-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 80% of the trials, whereas in left-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 20% of the trials. The ratio of the contrasts remained as above (2:2:2:2:1). Whether the first biased block in a session was left or right was randomly chosen, and blocks were then alternated. The length of a block was drawn from an exponential distribution with scale parameter of 60 trials, but truncated to lie between 20 and 100 trials.\\n\\nThe automated shaping protocol for training involved two collections of sessions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. They also experienced a debiasing protocol, which was intended to dissuade them from persisting with just one of the choices. Once they were performing sufficiently well on all non-zero contrasts, they were faced with the biased blocks. When, in turn, performance on those was adequate (including on 0% contrast trials, which are informed by the block), they graduated to recording. Supplementary Figure 8a shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the first and second collections (these were not correlated). Supplementary Figure 8b shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the second collection and the performance during the recording sessions. These were also not correlated.\\n36\\t\\n37\\tInclusion criteria\\n38\\t\\n39\\tWe applied a set of inclusion criteria to sessions, probes and neurons to ensure data quality. Supplementary Table 1 lists the consequences of these criteria for the number of sessions and probes that passed the criteria.\\n40\\tSessions and insertions\\n41\\t\\n42\\tEach Neuropixels insertion was repeated in at least two laboratories, with reproducibility of outcomes across laboratories verified with extensive analyses that we have previously reported25.\\n43\\t\\n44\\tSessions were included in the data release if the mice performed at least 250 trials, with a performance of at least 90% correct on 100% contrast trials for both left and right blocks, and, to be able to analyse the feedback variable, if there were at least 3 trials with incorrect choices (after applying the trial exclusions below). Furthermore, sessions were included in the release only if they reached threshold on a collection of hardware tests (definitions are available from GiHub (https://int-brain-lab.github.io/iblenv/_autosummary/ibllib.qc.task_metrics.html)).\\n45\\t\\n46\\tInsertions were excluded if the neural data failed the whole recording per visually assessed criteria of the ‘Recording Inclusion metrics and Guidelines for Optimal Reproducibility’ (RIGOR) from ref. 25, by presenting major artefacts (see examples in ref. 28) or if the probe tract could not be recovered during the histology procedure. Furthermore, only insertions for which alignments had been resolved (see appendix 6 of ref. 25 for definitions) were used in this study.\\n47\\t\\n48\\tAfter applying these criteria, a total of 459 sessions, 699 insertions and 621,733 neurons remained, constituting the publicly released dataset.\\n49\\tTrials\\n50\\t\\n51\\tFor the analyses presented here, trials were excluded if one of the following trial events could not be detected: choice, probabilityLeft, feebackType, feeback times, stimON times and firstMovement times. Trials were further excluded if the time between stimulus onset and the first movement of the wheel (the first wheel-movement time) were outside the range of 0.08–2.00 s.\\n52\\tNeurons and brain regions\\n53\\t\\n54\\tNeurons generated by the spike-sorting pipeline were excluded from the analyses presented here if they failed one of the three criteria described in ref. 28 (the single unit computed metrics of RIGOR25): amplitude > 50 μV; noise cut-off < 20 μV; and refractory period violation. Neurons that passed these criteria were termed well-isolated neurons (or often just ‘neurons’) in this study. Out of the 621,733 units collected, 75,708 were considered well-isolated neurons. Final analyses were additionally restricted to regions that were designated grey matter in the adult mouse Allen Common Coordinate framework6, contained at least five well-isolated neurons per session and were recorded from in at least two such sessions.\\n55\\t\\n56\\tVideo analysis\\n57\\t\\n58\\tWe briefly describe the video analysis pipeline (full details can be found in ref. 105). The recording rigs contained three cameras: one called ‘left’ at full resolution (1,280 × 1,024) and 60 Hz, filming the mouse from one side; one called ‘right’, filming the mouse symmetrically from the other side at half resolution (640 × 512) and 150 Hz; and one called ‘body’ at half resolution and 30 Hz, filming the body of the mouse from above. We developed several quality-control metrics to detect raw video issues such as poor illumination (as infrared light bulbs broke) or accidental misplacement of the cameras105.\\n59\\t\\n60\\tWe computed the motion energy (the mean across pixels of the absolute value of the difference between adjacent frames) of the whisker pad areas in the ‘left’ and ‘right’ videos (Fig. 1d). The whisker pad area was empirically defined using a rectangular bounding box anchored between the nose tip and the eye, both found using DeepLabCut106 (DLC; see more below). This metric quantifies motion in the whisker pad area and has a temporal resolution of the respective camera.\\n61\\t\\n62\\tWe also performed markerless pose estimation of body parts using DLC31, which is used in a fully automated pipeline in IBL (v.2.1) to track various body parts such as the paws, nose, tongue and pupil (Fig. 1d). In all analyses using DLC estimates, we excluded predictions with likelihood < 0.9. Furthermore, we developed several quality-control metrics for the DLC traces105.\\n63\\t\\n64\\tOverview of decoding\\n65\\t\\n66\\tWe performed a decoding analysis to measure how much information the activity of populations of neurons contained about task variables such as stimulus side and choice. To do this we, used cross-validated, maximum-likelihood regression with L1 regularization (to zero out the contribution from noisy neurons). The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). These factors are discussed further below and include a variety of behavioural and task variables: stimulus side, choice, feedback and wheel speed and velocity. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions. The P values for all regions were then subjected to FDR correction for multiple comparisons at q = 0.01.\\n67\\t\\n68\\tDecoding target variables\\n69\\t\\n70\\tStimulus side, choice and feedback were treated as binary target variables for logistic regression. For stimulus side, trials that had zero contrast were excluded. We used the LogisticRegression module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 20,000 maximum iterations, “l1” penalty, “liblinear” solver and “fit_intercept” set to True. We balanced decoder classes by weighting samples by the inverse of the class frequency, 1/(2Pi,class). Decoding performance was evaluated using the balanced accuracy of classification, which is the average of the recall probabilities for the two classes. Supplementary Figure 9 shows histograms of the regression coefficients for all the variables.\\n71\\t\\n72\\tWheel values (speed and velocity) change over the course of a trial, unlike the previous decoding targets, and we therefore had to treat these target variables differently. We averaged wheel values in nonoverlapping 20-ms bins, starting 200 ms before first wheel-movement time and ending at 1,000 ms after first wheel-movement time. Spike counts were similarly binned. The target value for a given bin (ending at time t) was decoded from spikes in a preceding (causal) window spanning W bins (ending at times t, …, t-W). Therefore, if decoding from n neurons, there were (W + 1)n predictors of the target variable in a given bin. In practice, we used W = 10. To decode these continuous-valued targets, we performed linear regression using the Lasso module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 1,000 maximum iterations and “fit_intercept” set to True.
