QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS Data processing IBL trial-aligned dataset For choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also  align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the  stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study, 27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel  movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike  counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5, 77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion en- ergy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending  at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we  similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session. IBL trial-unaligned dataset We focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental  trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align  neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets  to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials,  capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials. ll OPEN ACCESS   Article e8 Neuron 114, 1–16.e1–e11, February 4, 2026 Please cite this article in press as: Zhang et al., Exploiting correlations across trials and behavioral sessions to improve neural decoding, Neuron (2025),  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.10.026 Allen dataset To use reduced-rank regression models, we decode 3 behavior variables: Gabors, static gratings, and running speed. The Gabors  variable has 3 discrete orientation classes, while the static gratings variable has 6. Running speed, in contrast, is a continuous trial- unaligned variable recorded during periods of spontaneous behavior. For Gabors and static gratings, we align trials to the respective  stimulus onset and extract neural activity within a 200 ms window around the onset. \\n\\n===== 433  2728\\nuced-rank regression model that shares behaviorally  relevant neural structure across sessions and a multi-session state-space model that captures behavioral  structure across trials and sessions. On 433 sessions spanning 270 brain regions in the International Brain  Laboratory (IBL) mouse Neuropixels dataset, our decoders outperform traditional approaches on four behav- iors, with results generalizing across datasets, species, and tasks. Unlike deep learning methods, our models  are efficient and interpretable, providing low-dimensional neural representations, task-related single-neuron  contributions, and brain-wide timescales of neural activation. INTRODUCTION Neural decoding is a critical tool for understanding the relation- ship between neural activity and behavior. Traditional neural de- coders operate on a single-trial, single-session basis, 1,2 modeling  neural-behavioral relationships within individual trials. However,  they ignore correlations across trials and sessions in both neural  and behavioral data, missing opportunities to exploit the rich  structure of large-scale datasets spanning multiple sessions,  animals, and brain regions. Similar neural activities emerge across experimental sessions  when animals perform the same task. 3–6 Leveraging such inter- session neural similarities offers an opportunity to improve sin- gle-session decoding, 7–9 but direct sharing is difficult since  each session records different neurons. An alternative approach  is to capture population-level variations via their correlation  structures in neural latents across sessions. Previous unsuper- vised and self-supervised studies follow this strategy to estimate  shared neural dynamics, 10–13 although the learned latents often  lack behavioral relevance and thus require fine-tuning for decod- ing. Supervised approaches can instead learn behaviorally rele- vant neural representations across sessions, but existing  methods 14,15 demand heavy computation and produce complex  black-box models. A lightweight, interpretable model is therefore  needed to share behaviorally relevant neural variations across  sessions. Animal behavior depends not only on the current task but also  on prior experiences. For example, Ashwood et al. 16 show that  mouse decisions reflect internal states persisting across tens  to hundreds of trials, well captured by hidden Markov models  (HMMs). These latent states are reproducible across animals  and sessions, and many experiments exhibit similar trial-to-trial  correlations. Accounting for these behavioral correlations, along- side inter-session neural similarities, can potentially improve  decoding. Moreover, inferring these latent sta\\n\\n===== 433  6699\\n black-box models, our methods are simple,  interpretable, and easy to fit. We evaluate the proposed ap- proaches on International Brain Laboratory (IBL) mouse Neuro- pixels recordings 17,18 spanning 433 sessions and 270 brain  regions, as well as on the Allen Institute Neuropixels visual cod- ing dataset 19 and a primate random target-reaching task with  Utah arrays. 20 Across datasets, species, and tasks, our models  improve decoding accuracy. They are also computationally effi- cient, allowing us to create a brain-wide map of behaviorally rele- vant timescales and identify task-related neurons. RESULTS Formulation of the neural data-sharing model Our goal is to decode behavior y ∈ ℝ P from spike-sorted,  temporally binned spike counts. For each trial k, neural activity  has size N × T, where N is the number of neurons and T the num- ber of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each  divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For  each trial, we constructed X ∈ ℝ N×T by aggregating spike  counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate d ∈ ℝ P of  the true behavior y ∈ ℝ P . y is constant within a trial (‘‘per-trial  decoding’’); when P = T, y varies across time (‘‘per-timestep  decoding’’). For simplicity, we first present the model assuming  y is scalar (P = 1). Traditional single-session decoders use full-rank models with  an unconstrained weight matrix W ∈ ℝ N×T : d = f(vec(X) ⊤ vec(W) + b); (Equation 1) where vec( ⋅) denotes the vectorization (flattening) operator, and  b ∈ ℝ is a bias term. For large N and T, the number of parame- ters grows quickly, making such models prone to overfitting.  To mitigate overfitting, we impose a low-rank constraint on the  weight matrix by factorizing it into two smaller matrices: d = f(vec(X) ⊤ vec(UV) + b); (Equation 2) where U ∈ ℝ N×R and V ∈ ℝ R×T are low-rank bases capturing  neural and temporal components of W. This RRR lowers the  parameter count from N × T (Equation 1) to R(N + T), with R <  min(N; T). The function f may be linear or nonlinear, depending  on the application. Note that the formulation in Equation 2 differs  from standard reduced-rank regression previously applied to  predict neural responses 21 ; see STAR Methods for details. The parameters U, V, and b can be estimated via automatic  differentiation or closed-form solutions. When f is the identity  function (linear model), closed-form solutions exist. In particular,  U defines a subspace that maximizes the correlation between  neural activity X and behavior y while capturing the main varia- tions in y. Consequently, the RRR can be interpreted as a latent  variable model, with rank R specifying the number of latent\\n\\n===== 433  18801\\nd implementation details, see  STAR Methods section ‘‘BMM-HMM: model details’’ and ‘‘LG- AR1: model details.’’ Learning behaviorally relevant neural variations across  sessions We apply our models to 433 IBL sessions, 17 covering 270 brain  regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel  speed, and whisker motion energy. While our main experiments  focus on IBL data, the methods are broadly applicable to neural  activity, with consistent temporal structure and behaviors exhib- iting trial-to-trial correlations. In the IBL experiments, mice rotate  a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as  their choice (Figure 1A). For the first 90 trials, the stimulus ap- pears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subse- quent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. 17,18  Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allow- ing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior)  about stimulus location. 27 Additionally, wheel speed and whisker  motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker mo- tion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference be- tween adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored  between nose tip and eye. 34 Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time- varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections  ‘‘data processing’’ and ‘‘hyperparameter selection’’ for details.  The RRR improves decoding by projecting neural activity onto a  low-dimensional subspace that emphasizes behaviorally relevant  variability. Unlike principal-component analysis (PCA), 35 which  captures both relevant and irrelevant components, 36,37 RRR fo- cuses on neural representations most predictive of behavior. 38  This supervised dimensionality reduction disentangles behavior- ally relevant dynamics more effectively than unsupervised  methods such as PCA or demixed PCA 38 (see STAR Methods).  To illustrate, we compare PCA and RRR projections for decod- ing the binary choice variable. Figure 2A shows single-session  projections, where RRR better separates behavioral classes  than PCA. Using k-means clustering and the adjusted Rand index  (ARI), 39,40 we find that RRR (M) produces more discriminative  neural representations by leveraging shared structure across  sessions, reducing overfitting and enhancing generalizability. In  Figures 2B and 2C, RRR (M) achieves higher ARI and decoding  accuracy than single-session RRR (p < 0:002 via bootstrap re- sampling; see STAR Methods), confirming the significance of  these gains. The RRR also improves decoding of continuous behaviors—  prior, wheel speed, and whi\\n\\n===== 433  37944\\ns, 24–26 with motor and sensory areas  operating faster than cognition-related regions. Yet, how these  dynamics relate to behavior remains largely unexplored. To  investigate, we fit the RRR (MR) on 433 sessions across 270  brain areas to decode choice and prior and use the first rank of  the region-specific temporal basis V j as each region’s timescale.  Figure 7A shows distinct activation timescales across regions,  including the gigantocellular reticular nucleus (GRN), motor cor- tex (MOp), nucleus accumbens (ACB), amygdala complex (CEA),  CA1 in the hippocampus, basomedial amygdala (BMA), and  VISa. Peak activation (peak) is the highest point of the curve,  and activation duration (width) is the interval spanning 90% of  the peak height. Although peak activation occurs at similar times  following stimulus onset, ACB and BMA exhibit more prolonged  activation, compared with other regions. We use each area’s peak activation time and duration  (Figure 7A) to compare behaviorally relevant timescales. For  choice decoding, most regions peak within 1.5 s of stimulus  onset, consistent with the ‘‘reaction time’’ (stimulus onset to initial  movement; see Figure 1C in IBL et al. 18 ). Figure 7B (top row)  shows broadly similar peak times, except for the olfactory bulb  and cerebellum, which may activate later upon receiving water  reward. Figure 7C (top row) shows shorter activation durations  in hindbrain regions, compared with forebrain and midbrain.  For prior decoding, Figure 7B (bottom row) shows earlier cortical  activation and delayed cerebellar activation, while Figure 7C (bot- tom row) shows longer activation durations in cortex and thal- amus. White areas mark regions excluded from decoding  because of missing behavioral data. In addition to showing activation timing and duration (Figures 7B  and 7C), we analyze how much behavioral information is decod- able from each region. While IBL et al. 18 map decoding accuracy  using L2-regularized linear decoders, Figure 7D shows that the  RRR (MR), a more constrained and interpretable linear decoder  trained with more data, improves choice and prior decoding  across most regions. This suggests that regularized linear de- coders may not fully capture decision-related information in  each region, potentially affecting interpretations based on them.  In the STAR Methods, we confirm that the RRR (MR) improves  information decoding from each region relative to the baseline  linear decoder. To control for spurious correlations, 41 we  generate null distributions using ‘‘imposter sessions. 18 ’’ Analysis  of representative regions (PO, LP, DG, CA1, and VISa) in Figure 5. Quantitative comparison of the proposed \\n\\n===== 270 brain 2750\\nodel that shares behaviorally  relevant neural structure across sessions and a multi-session state-space model that captures behavioral  structure across trials and sessions. On 433 sessions spanning 270 brain regions in the International Brain  Laboratory (IBL) mouse Neuropixels dataset, our decoders outperform traditional approaches on four behav- iors, with results generalizing across datasets, species, and tasks. Unlike deep learning methods, our models  are efficient and interpretable, providing low-dimensional neural representations, task-related single-neuron  contributions, and brain-wide timescales of neural activation. INTRODUCTION Neural decoding is a critical tool for understanding the relation- ship between neural activity and behavior. Traditional neural de- coders operate on a single-trial, single-session basis, 1,2 modeling  neural-behavioral relationships within individual trials. However,  they ignore correlations across trials and sessions in both neural  and behavioral data, missing opportunities to exploit the rich  structure of large-scale datasets spanning multiple sessions,  animals, and brain regions. Similar neural activities emerge across experimental sessions  when animals perform the same task. 3–6 Leveraging such inter- session neural similarities offers an opportunity to improve sin- gle-session decoding, 7–9 but direct sharing is difficult since  each session records different neurons. An alternative approach  is to capture population-level variations via their correlation  structures in neural latents across sessions. Previous unsuper- vised and self-supervised studies follow this strategy to estimate  shared neural dynamics, 10–13 although the learned latents often  lack behavioral relevance and thus require fine-tuning for decod- ing. Supervised approaches can instead learn behaviorally rele- vant neural representations across sessions, but existing  methods 14,15 demand heavy computation and produce complex  black-box models. A lightweight, interpretable model is therefore  needed to share behaviorally relevant neural variations across  sessions. Animal behavior depends not only on the current task but also  on prior experiences. For example, Ashwood et al. 16 show that  mouse decisions reflect internal states persisting across tens  to hundreds of trials, well captured by hidden Markov models  (HMMs). These latent states are reproducible across animals  and sessions, and many experiments exhibit similar trial-to-trial  correlations. Accounting for these behavioral correlations, along- side inter-session neural similarities, can potentially improve  decoding. Moreover, inferring these latent states reveals the in- te\\n\\n===== 270 brain 6716\\n, our methods are simple,  interpretable, and easy to fit. We evaluate the proposed ap- proaches on International Brain Laboratory (IBL) mouse Neuro- pixels recordings 17,18 spanning 433 sessions and 270 brain  regions, as well as on the Allen Institute Neuropixels visual cod- ing dataset 19 and a primate random target-reaching task with  Utah arrays. 20 Across datasets, species, and tasks, our models  improve decoding accuracy. They are also computationally effi- cient, allowing us to create a brain-wide map of behaviorally rele- vant timescales and identify task-related neurons. RESULTS Formulation of the neural data-sharing model Our goal is to decode behavior y ∈ ℝ P from spike-sorted,  temporally binned spike counts. For each trial k, neural activity  has size N × T, where N is the number of neurons and T the num- ber of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each  divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For  each trial, we constructed X ∈ ℝ N×T by aggregating spike  counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate d ∈ ℝ P of  the true behavior y ∈ ℝ P . y is constant within a trial (‘‘per-trial  decoding’’); when P = T, y varies across time (‘‘per-timestep  decoding’’). For simplicity, we first present the model assuming  y is scalar (P = 1). Traditional single-session decoders use full-rank models with  an unconstrained weight matrix W ∈ ℝ N×T : d = f(vec(X) ⊤ vec(W) + b); (Equation 1) where vec( ⋅) denotes the vectorization (flattening) operator, and  b ∈ ℝ is a bias term. For large N and T, the number of parame- ters grows quickly, making such models prone to overfitting.  To mitigate overfitting, we impose a low-rank constraint on the  weight matrix by factorizing it into two smaller matrices: d = f(vec(X) ⊤ vec(UV) + b); (Equation 2) where U ∈ ℝ N×R and V ∈ ℝ R×T are low-rank bases capturing  neural and temporal components of W. This RRR lowers the  parameter count from N × T (Equation 1) to R(N + T), with R <  min(N; T). The function f may be linear or nonlinear, depending  on the application. Note that the formulation in Equation 2 differs  from standard reduced-rank regression previously applied to  predict neural responses 21 ; see STAR Methods for details. The parameters U, V, and b can be estimated via automatic  differentiation or closed-form solutions. When f is the identity  function (linear model), closed-form solutions exist. In particular,  U defines a subspace that maximizes the correlation between  neural activity X and behavior y while capturing the main varia- tions in y. Consequently, the RRR can be interpreted as a latent  variable model, with rank R specifying the number of latent vari- ables need\\n\\n===== 270 brain 18831\\n STAR Methods section ‘‘BMM-HMM: model details’’ and ‘‘LG- AR1: model details.’’ Learning behaviorally relevant neural variations across  sessions We apply our models to 433 IBL sessions, 17 covering 270 brain  regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel  speed, and whisker motion energy. While our main experiments  focus on IBL data, the methods are broadly applicable to neural  activity, with consistent temporal structure and behaviors exhib- iting trial-to-trial correlations. In the IBL experiments, mice rotate  a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as  their choice (Figure 1A). For the first 90 trials, the stimulus ap- pears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subse- quent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. 17,18  Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allow- ing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior)  about stimulus location. 27 Additionally, wheel speed and whisker  motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker mo- tion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference be- tween adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored  between nose tip and eye. 34 Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time- varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections  ‘‘data processing’’ and ‘‘hyperparameter selection’’ for details.  The RRR improves decoding by projecting neural activity onto a  low-dimensional subspace that emphasizes behaviorally relevant  variability. Unlike principal-component analysis (PCA), 35 which  captures both relevant and irrelevant components, 36,37 RRR fo- cuses on neural representations most predictive of behavior. 38  This supervised dimensionality reduction disentangles behavior- ally relevant dynamics more effectively than unsupervised  methods such as PCA or demixed PCA 38 (see STAR Methods).  To illustrate, we compare PCA and RRR projections for decod- ing the binary choice variable. Figure 2A shows single-session  projections, where RRR better separates behavioral classes  than PCA. Using k-means clustering and the adjusted Rand index  (ARI), 39,40 we find that RRR (M) produces more discriminative  neural representations by leveraging shared structure across  sessions, reducing overfitting and enhancing generalizability. In  Figures 2B and 2C, RRR (M) achieves higher ARI and decoding  accuracy than single-session RRR (p < 0:002 via bootstrap re- sampling; see STAR Methods), confirming the significance of  these gains. QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS Data processing IBL trial-aligned dataset For choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also  align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the  stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study, 27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel  movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike  counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5, 77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion en- ergy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending  at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we  similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session. IBL trial-unaligned dataset We focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental  trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align  neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets  to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials,  capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials. ll OPEN ACCESS   Article e8 Neuron 114, 1–16.e1–e11, February 4, 2026 Please cite this article in press as: Zhang et al., Exploiting correlations across trials and behavioral sessions to improve neural decoding, Neuron (2025),  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.10.026 Allen dataset To use reduced-rank regression models, we decode 3 behavior variables: Gabors, static gratings, and running speed. The Gabors  variable has 3 discrete orientation classes, while the static gratings variable has 6. Running speed, in contrast, is a continuous trial- unaligned variable recorded during periods of spontaneous behavior. For Gabors and static gratings, we align trials to the respective  stimulus onset and extract neural activity within a 200 ms window around the onset. \\n\\n===== 433  2728\\nuced-rank regression model that shares behaviorally  relevant neural structure across sessions and a multi-session state-space model that captures behavioral  structure across trials and sessions. The RRR also improves decoding of continuous behaviors—  prior, wheel speed, and whi\\n\\n===== 433  37944\\ns, 24–26 with motor and sensory areas  operating faster than cognition-related regions. Yet, how these  dynamics relate to behavior remains largely unexplored. To  investigate, we fit the RRR (MR) on 433 sessions across 270  brain areas to decode choice and prior and use the first rank of  the region-specific temporal basis V j as each region’s timescale.  Figure 7A shows distinct activation timescales across regions,  including the gigantocellular reticular nucleus (GRN), motor cor- tex (MOp), nucleus accumbens (ACB), amygdala complex (CEA),  CA1 in the hippocampus, basomedial amygdala (BMA), and  VISa. Peak activation (peak) is the highest point of the curve,  and activation duration (width) is the interval spanning 90% of  the peak height. Although peak activation occurs at similar times  following stimulus onset, ACB and BMA exhibit more prolonged  activation, compared with other regions. We use each area’s peak activation time and duration  (Figure 7A) to compare behaviorally relevant timescales. For  choice decoding, most regions peak within 1.5 s of stimulus  onset, consistent with the ‘‘reaction time’’ (stimulus onset to initial  movement; see Figure 1C in IBL et al. 18 ). Figure 7B (top row)  shows broadly similar peak times, except for the olfactory bulb  and cerebellum, which may activate later upon receiving water  reward. Figure 7C (top row) shows shorter activation durations  in hindbrain regions, compared with forebrain and midbrain.  For prior decoding, Figure 7B (bottom row) shows earlier cortical  activation and delayed cerebellar activation, while Figure 7C (bot- tom row) shows longer activation durations in cortex and thal- amus. White areas mark regions excluded from decoding  because of missing behavioral data. In addition to showing activation timing and duration (Figures 7B  and 7C), we analyze how much behavioral information is decod- able from each region. While IBL et al. 18 map decoding accuracy  using L2-regularized linear decoders, Figure 7D shows that the  RRR (MR), a more constrained and interpretable linear decoder  trained with more data, improves choice and prior decoding  across most regions. This suggests that regularized linear de- coders may not fully capture decision-related information in  each region, potentially affecting interpretations based on them.  In the STAR Methods, we confirm that the RRR (MR) improves  information decoding from each region relative to the baseline  linear decoder. To control for spurious correlations, 41 we  generate null distributions using ‘‘imposter sessions. 18 ’’ Analysis  of representative regions (PO, LP, DG, CA1, and VISa) in Figure 5. QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS Data processing IBL trial-aligned dataset For choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also  align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the  stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study, 27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel  movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike  counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5, 77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion en- ergy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending  at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we  similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session. IBL trial-unaligned dataset We focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental  trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align  neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets  to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials,  capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials. ll OPEN ACCESS   Article e8 Neuron 114, 1–16.e1–e11, February 4, 2026 Please cite this article in press as: Zhang et al., Exploiting correlations across trials and behavioral sessions to improve neural decoding, Neuron (2025),  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.10.026 Allen dataset To use reduced-rank regression models, we decode 3 behavior variables: Gabors, static gratings, and running speed. The Gabors  variable has 3 discrete orientation classes, while the static gratings variable has 6. Running speed, in contrast, is a continuous trial- unaligned variable recorded during periods of spontaneous behavior. On 433 sessions spanning 270 brain regions in the International Brain  Laboratory (IBL) mouse Neuropixels dataset, our decoders outperform traditional approaches on four behav- iors, with results generalizing across datasets, species, and tasks. Unlike deep learning methods, our models  are efficient and interpretable, providing low-dimensional neural representations, task-related single-neuron  contributions, and brain-wide timescales of neural activation. INTRODUCTION Neural decoding is a critical tool for understanding the relation- ship between neural activity and behavior. Traditional neural de- coders operate on a single-trial, single-session basis, 1,2 modeling  neural-behavioral relationships within individual trials. However,  they ignore correlations across trials and sessions in both neural  and behavioral data, missing opportunities to exploit the rich  structure of large-scale datasets spanning multiple sessions,  animals, and brain regions. Similar neural activities emerge across experimental sessions  when animals perform the same task. 3–6 Leveraging such inter- session neural similarities offers an opportunity to improve sin- gle-session decoding, 7–9 but direct sharing is difficult since  each session records different neurons. An alternative approach  is to capture population-level variations via their correlation  structures in neural latents across sessions. Previous unsuper- vised and self-supervised studies follow this strategy to estimate  shared neural dynamics, 10–13 although the learned latents often  lack behavioral relevance and thus require fine-tuning for decod- ing. Supervised approaches can instead learn behaviorally rele- vant neural representations across sessions, but existing  methods 14,15 demand heavy computation and produce complex  black-box models. A lightweight, interpretable model is therefore  needed to share behaviorally relevant neural variations across  sessions. Animal behavior depends not only on the current task but also  on prior experiences. For example, Ashwood et al. 16 show that  mouse decisions reflect internal states persisting across tens  to hundreds of trials, well captured by hidden Markov models  (HMMs). These latent states are reproducible across animals  and sessions, and many experiments exhibit similar trial-to-trial  correlations. Accounting for these behavioral correlations, along- side inter-session neural similarities, can potentially improve  decoding. Moreover, inferring these latent sta\\n\\n===== 433  6699\\n black-box models, our methods are simple,  interpretable, and easy to fit. We evaluate the proposed ap- proaches on International Brain Laboratory (IBL) mouse Neuro- pixels recordings 17,18 spanning 433 sessions and 270 brain  regions, as well as on the Allen Institute Neuropixels visual cod- ing dataset 19 and a primate random target-reaching task with  Utah arrays. 20 Across datasets, species, and tasks, our models  improve decoding accuracy. They are also computationally effi- cient, allowing us to create a brain-wide map of behaviorally rele- vant timescales and identify task-related neurons. RESULTS Formulation of the neural data-sharing model Our goal is to decode behavior y ∈ ℝ P from spike-sorted,  temporally binned spike counts. For each trial k, neural activity  has size N × T, where N is the number of neurons and T the num- ber of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each  divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For  each trial, we constructed X ∈ ℝ N×T by aggregating spike  counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate d ∈ ℝ P of  the true behavior y ∈ ℝ P . y is constant within a trial (‘‘per-trial  decoding’’); when P = T, y varies across time (‘‘per-timestep  decoding’’). For simplicity, we first present the model assuming  y is scalar (P = 1). Traditional single-session decoders use full-rank models with  an unconstrained weight matrix W ∈ ℝ N×T : d = f(vec(X) ⊤ vec(W) + b); (Equation 1) where vec( ⋅) denotes the vectorization (flattening) operator, and  b ∈ ℝ is a bias term. For large N and T, the number of parame- ters grows quickly, making such models prone to overfitting.  To mitigate overfitting, we impose a low-rank constraint on the  weight matrix by factorizing it into two smaller matrices: d = f(vec(X) ⊤ vec(UV) + b); (Equation 2) where U ∈ ℝ N×R and V ∈ ℝ R×T are low-rank bases capturing  neural and temporal components of W. This RRR lowers the  parameter count from N × T (Equation 1) to R(N + T), with R <  min(N; T). The function f may be linear or nonlinear, depending  on the application. Note that the formulation in Equation 2 differs  from standard reduced-rank regression previously applied to  predict neural responses 21 ; see STAR Methods for details. The parameters U, V, and b can be estimated via automatic  differentiation or closed-form solutions. When f is the identity  function (linear model), closed-form solutions exist. In particular,  U defines a subspace that maximizes the correlation between  neural activity X and behavior y while capturing the main varia- tions in y. Consequently, the RRR can be interpreted as a latent  variable model, with rank R specifying the number of latent\\n\\n===== 433  18801\\nd implementation details, see  STAR Methods section ‘‘BMM-HMM: model details’’ and ‘‘LG- AR1: model details.’’ Learning behaviorally relevant neural variations across  sessions We apply our models to 433 IBL sessions, 17 covering 270 brain  regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel  speed, and whisker motion energy. While our main experiments  focus on IBL data, the methods are broadly applicable to neural  activity, with consistent temporal structure and behaviors exhib- iting trial-to-trial correlations. In the IBL experiments, mice rotate  a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as  their choice (Figure 1A). For the first 90 trials, the stimulus ap- pears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subse- quent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. 17,18  Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allow- ing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior)  about stimulus location. 27 Additionally, wheel speed and whisker  motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker mo- tion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference be- tween adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored  between nose tip and eye. 34 Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time- varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections  ‘‘data processing’’ and ‘‘hyperparameter selection’’ for details.  The RRR improves decoding by projecting neural activity onto a  low-dimensional subspace that emphasizes behaviorally relevant  variability. Unlike principal-component analysis (PCA), 35 which  captures both relevant and irrelevant components, 36,37 RRR fo- cuses on neural representations most predictive of behavior. 38  This supervised dimensionality reduction disentangles behavior- ally relevant dynamics more effectively than unsupervised  methods such as PCA or demixed PCA 38 (see STAR Methods).  To illustrate, we compare PCA and RRR projections for decod- ing the binary choice variable. Figure 2A shows single-session  projections, where RRR better separates behavioral classes  than PCA. Using k-means clustering and the adjusted Rand index  (ARI), 39,40 we find that RRR (M) produces more discriminative  neural representations by leveraging shared structure across  sessions, reducing overfitting and enhancing generalizability. In  Figures 2B and 2C, RRR (M) achieves higher ARI and decoding  accuracy than single-session RRR (p < 0:002 via bootstrap re- sampling; see STAR Methods), confirming the significance of  these gains. The RRR also improves decoding of continuous behaviors—  prior, wheel speed, and whi\\n\\n===== 433  37944\\ns, 24–26 with motor and sensory areas  operating faster than cognition-related regions. Yet, how these  dynamics relate to behavior remains largely unexplored. To  investigate, we fit the RRR (MR) on 433 sessions across 270  brain areas to decode choice and prior and use the first rank of  the region-specific temporal basis V j as each region’s timescale.  Figure 7A shows distinct activation timescales across regions,  including the gigantocellular reticular nucleus (GRN), motor cor- tex (MOp), nucleus accumbens (ACB), amygdala complex (CEA),  CA1 in the hippocampus, basomedial amygdala (BMA), and  VISa. Peak activation (peak) is the highest point of the curve,  and activation duration (width) is the interval spanning 90% of  the peak height. Although peak activation occurs at similar times  following stimulus onset, ACB and BMA exhibit more prolonged  activation, compared with other regions. We use each area’s peak activation time and duration  (Figure 7A) to compare behaviorally relevant timescales. For  choice decoding, most regions peak within 1.5 s of stimulus  onset, consistent with the ‘‘reaction time’’ (stimulus onset to initial  movement; see Figure 1C in IBL et al. 18 ). Figure 7B (top row)  shows broadly similar peak times, except for the olfactory bulb  and cerebellum, which may activate later upon receiving water  reward. Figure 7C (top row) shows shorter activation durations  in hindbrain regions, compared with forebrain and midbrain.  For prior decoding, Figure 7B (bottom row) shows earlier cortical  activation and delayed cerebellar activation, while Figure 7C (bot- tom row) shows longer activation durations in cortex and thal- amus. White areas mark regions excluded from decoding  because of missing behavioral data. In addition to showing activation timing and duration (Figures 7B  and 7C), we analyze how much behavioral information is decod- able from each region. While IBL et al. 18 map decoding accuracy  using L2-regularized linear decoders, Figure 7D shows that the  RRR (MR), a more constrained and interpretable linear decoder  trained with more data, improves choice and prior decoding  across most regions. This suggests that regularized linear de- coders may not fully capture decision-related information in  each region, potentially affecting interpretations based on them.  In the STAR Methods, we confirm that the RRR (MR) improves  information decoding from each region relative to the baseline  linear decoder. To control for spurious correlations, 41 we  generate null distributions using ‘‘imposter sessions. 18 ’’ Analysis  of representative regions (PO, LP, DG, CA1, and VISa) in Figure 5. Accounting for these behavioral correlations, along- side inter-session neural similarities, can potentially improve  decoding. Moreover, inferring these latent sta\\n\\n===== 433  6699\\n black-box models, our methods are simple,  interpretable, and easy to fit. We evaluate the proposed ap- proaches on International Brain Laboratory (IBL) mouse Neuro- pixels recordings 17,18 spanning 433 sessions and 270 brain  regions, as well as on the Allen Institute Neuropixels visual cod- ing dataset 19 and a primate random target-reaching task with  Utah arrays. 20 Across datasets, species, and tasks, our models  improve decoding accuracy. They are also computationally effi- cient, allowing us to create a brain-wide map of behaviorally rele- vant timescales and identify task-related neurons. RESULTS Formulation of the neural data-sharing model Our goal is to decode behavior y ∈ ℝ P from spike-sorted,  temporally binned spike counts. For each trial k, neural activity  has size N × T, where N is the number of neurons and T the num- ber of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each  divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For  each trial, we constructed X ∈ ℝ N×T by aggregating spike  counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate d ∈ ℝ P of  the true behavior y ∈ ℝ P . y is constant within a trial (‘‘per-trial  decoding’’); when P = T, y varies across time (‘‘per-timestep  decoding’’). For simplicity, we first present the model assuming  y is scalar (P = 1). Traditional single-session decoders use full-rank models with  an unconstrained weight matrix W ∈ ℝ N×T : d = f(vec(X) ⊤ vec(W) + b); (Equation 1) where vec( ⋅) denotes the vectorization (flattening) operator, and  b ∈ ℝ is a bias term. For large N and T, the number of parame- ters grows quickly, making such models prone to overfitting.  To mitigate overfitting, we impose a low-rank constraint on the  weight matrix by factorizing it into two smaller matrices: d = f(vec(X) ⊤ vec(UV) + b); (Equation 2) where U ∈ ℝ N×R and V ∈ ℝ R×T are low-rank bases capturing  neural and temporal components of W. This RRR lowers the  parameter count from N × T (Equation 1) to R(N + T), with R <  min(N; T). The function f may be linear or nonlinear, depending  on the application. Note that the formulation in Equation 2 differs  from standard reduced-rank regression previously applied to  predict neural responses 21 ; see STAR Methods for details. The parameters U, V, and b can be estimated via automatic  differentiation or closed-form solutions. under\\n/app/data is read directly.\\n\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n\\nimport argparse\\nimport os\\nimport pickle\\nimport sys\\nimport time\\nimport traceback\\nimport warnings\\nfrom concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, as_completed\\n\\nwarnings.filterwarnings('ignore')\\n\\nimport numpy as np\\nimport pandas as pd\\n\\n# Reference code from the method paper; reused rather than re-implemented where possible.\\nREFCODE = '/app/code/code_zhang2025/src'\\nsys.path.insert(0, REFCODE)\\n\\nfrom one.api import ONE                                     # noqa: E402\\nfrom brainbox.io.one import SessionLoader, SpikeSortingLoader  # noqa: E402\\nfrom iblatlas.regions import BrainRegions                    # noqa: E402\\nfrom scipy.interpolate import interp1d                       # noqa: E402\\n\\nfrom utils.ibl_data_utils import load_trials_and_mask, merge_probes  # noqa: E402\\n\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\n# Constants -- these mirror `params` in the reference caching script.\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\nONE_BASE_URL = 'https://openalyx.internationalbrainlab.org'\\nONE_CACHE_DIR = '/app/data/one_cache'\\nBWM_RELEASE_CSV = '/app/code/code_zhang2025/data/bwm_release.csv'\\n\\nALIGN_TIME = 'stimOn_times'\\nTIME_WINDOW = (-0.5, 1.5)          # seconds relative to the alignment event\\nBINSIZE = 0.02                     # seconds\\nNBINS = int(np.ceil((TIME_WINDOW[1] - TIME_WINDOW[0]) / BINSIZE))   # -> 100\\nMAX_TRIAL_LEN = 10.0               # `load_trials_and_mask(max_trial_len=10.0)` in the ref\\nQC_LABEL = 1.0                     # cluster['label'] >= 1  <=> IBL \\\"well-isolated neuron\\\"\\nNON_GREY_MATTER = ('root', 'void')  # Beryl acronyms that are not grey matter\\nMIN_TRIALS = 2                     # the target format needs >= 2 trials per session\\n\\nINPUT_NAMES = ['time_from_stimulus_onset', 'trial_number_in_block']\\nOUTPUT_NAMES = ['choice', 'prior_probability_left', 'wheel_speed', 'whisker_motion_energy']\\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\\n    ['left', 'right'],\\n    ['p(left)=0.2', 'p(left)=0.5', 'p(left)=0.8'],\\n    ['low', 'medium', 'high'],\\n    ['low', 'medium', 'high'],\\n]\\n\\n# Bin centres of the neural bins, relative to stimulus onset (seconds).\\nBIN_CENTRES = TIME_WINDOW[0] + BINSIZE * (np.arange(NBINS) + 0.5)\\n# Behaviour is sampled at the *right edge* of each bin, exactly as the reference\\n# `get_behavior_per_interval` does (`np.linspace(beg + binsize, end, n_bins)`).\\nBIN_RIGHT_EDGES = TIME_WINDOW[0] + BINSIZE * (np.arange(NBINS) + 1)\\n\\n\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\n# ONE access\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\ndef get_one():\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Build a ONE client against the staged local cache.\\n\\n    The default (remote) mode is used deliberately: it resolves datasets through the\\n    cached Alyx REST responses in `<cache>/.rest`, which know about the dataset revisions\\n    that are actually staged on disk (e.g. `alf/#2025-03-03#/_ibl_trials.table.pqt`).\\n    The copied `Brainwidemap` release table predates those revisions, so `mode='local'`\\n    silently fails to find the trials table.\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    return ONE(base_url=ONE_BASE_URL, silent=True, cache_dir=ONE_CACHE_DIR)\\n\\n\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\n# Neural data\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\ndef load_session_spikes(one, eid, pids, pnames):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Load and merge the spike sorting of every probe of a session.\\n\\n    Mirrors `ibl_data_utils.prepare_data`: each probe is loaded with\\n    `SpikeSortingLoader.load_spike_sorting` + `merge_clusters`, then probes are merged with\\n    the reference `merge_probes` helper (neurons of one session are pooled across probes\\n    because the probes are not statistically independent -- see the data paper,\\n    \\\"Overview of decoding\\\").\\n\\n    The reference additionally queries `raw_electrophysiology(band='ap', stream=True).fs`\\n    to record the AP sampling rate. That streams raw ephys over the network and is not\\n    used by any downstream computation, so it is skipped.\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    spikes_list, clusters_list = [], []\\n    for pid, pname in zip(pids, pnames):\\n        ssl = SpikeSortingLoader(pid=str(pid), one=one, eid=eid, pname=pname)\\n        sp, cl, ch = ssl.load_spike_sorting()\\n        if len(sp) == 0 or len(cl) == 0:\\n            continue\\n        cld = SpikeSortingLoader.merge_clusters(sp, cl, ch).to_df()\\n        cld['pid'] = str(pid)\\n        spikes_list.append(sp)\\n        clusters_list.append(cld)\\n    if not spikes_list:\\n        raise RuntimeError('no spike sorting could be loaded for this session')\\n    if len(spikes_list) == 1:\\n        return spikes_list[0], clusters_list[0]\\n    return merge_probes(spikes_list, clusters_list)\\n\\n\\ndef select_neurons(clusters, brain_regions):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Apply the data paper's neuron and region inclusion criteria.\\n\\n    * `label >= 1` keeps only \\\"well-isolated neurons\\\": in `ibllib`, `label` is the fraction\\n      of the three RIGOR single-unit metrics a cluster passes (amplitude > 50 uV,\\n      noise cut-off < 20 uV, refractory-period violation), so `label == 1` is exactly the\\n      data paper's criterion.\\n    * Beryl acronyms `root` / `void` are dropped, implementing the data paper's restriction\\n      to regions \\\"designated grey matter in the adult mouse Allen CCF\\\". The reference code\\n      makes the same exclusion in `MultiRegionDataModule.list_regions`.\\n\\n    Returns (keep_idx, beryl_acronyms_of_kept_neurons).\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    beryl = np.asarray(brain_regions.acronym2acronym(\\n        clusters['acronym'].to_numpy(), mapping='Beryl'))\\n    good = clusters['label'].to_numpy() >= QC_LABEL\\n    grey = ~np.isin(beryl, NON_GREY_MATTER)\\n    keep = np.nonzero(good & grey)[0]\\n    return keep, beryl[keep]\\n\\n\\ndef bin_spiking_data_fast(spike_times, spike_clusters, n_clusters, align_times):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Bin spikes into (n_trials, n_clusters, NBINS) counts.\\n\\n    Vectorised equivalent of the reference `bin_spiking_data` /\\n    `get_spike_data_per_interval`, which calls `iblutil.numerical.bincount2D` once per\\n    trial inside a multiprocessing pool. `bincount2D` assigns a sample to bin\\n    `floor((t - t_beg) / binsize)` over `[t_beg, t_end]` and the reference then truncates\\n    to the first `NBINS` columns, so a spike landing exactly on `t_end` is dropped. The\\n    same convention is reproduced here (spikes are taken from `[t_beg, t_end)` and bin\\n    indices outside `[0, NBINS)` are discarded).\\n\\n    Args:\\n        spike_times: (n_spikes,) spike times, sorted ascending.\\n        spike_clusters: (n_spikes,) cluster index in `[0, n_clusters)`.\\n        n_clusters: number of neurons.\\n        align_times: (n_trials,) alignment event times.\\n\\n    Returns:\\n        (n_trials, n_clusters, NBINS) uint8 array of spike counts.\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    beg = align_times + TIME_WINDOW[0]\\n    end = align_times + TIME_WINDOW[1]\\n    out = np.zeros((len(align_times), n_clusters, NBINS), dtype=np.uint8)\\n    finite = np.isfinite(beg) & np.isfinite(end)\\n    i0 = np.searchsorted(spike_times, np.where(finite, beg, np.inf), side='left')\\n    i1 = np.searchsorted(spike_times, np.where(finite, end, np.inf), side='left')\\n    for k in range(len(align_times)):\\n        if not finite[k]:\\n            continue\\n        t = spike_times[i0[k]:i1[k]]\\n        c = spike_clusters[i0[k]:i1[k]]\\n        b = np.floor((t - beg[k]) / BINSIZE).astype(np.int64)\\n        ok = (b >= 0) & (b < NBINS)\\n        counts = np.bincount(c[ok] * NBINS + b[ok], minlength=n_clusters * NBINS)\\n        np.clip(counts, 0, 255, out=counts)\\n        out[k] = counts.reshape(n_clusters, NBINS).astype(np.uint8)\\n    return out\\n\\n\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\n# Behaviour\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\ndef load_dynamic_behaviour(sess_loader):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Load the two time-varying behaviours the decoder has to predict.\\n\\n    Reproduces `ibl_data_utils.load_target_behavior`:\\n      * wheel speed  = |velocity| of the uniformly resampled (~1 kHz) wheel trace,\\n      * whisker motion energy = `whiskerMotionEnergy` of the **left** camera (60 Hz),\\n        falling back to the right camera (150 Hz) when the left one is unavailable --\\n        exactly the fallback in `ibl_data_utils.bin_behaviors`.\\n\\n    Returns {'wheel-speed': (times, values), 'whisker-motion-energy': (times, values)},\\n    plus the camera actually used.\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    out = {}\\n    sess_loader.load_wheel()\\n    out['wheel-speed'] = (sess_loader.wheel['times'].to_numpy(),\\n                          np.abs(sess_loader.wheel['velocity'].to_numpy()))\\n\\n    camera_used = None\\n    for view, key in (('left', 'leftCamera'), ('right', 'rightCamera')):\\n        try:\\n            sess_loader.load_motion_energy(views=[view])\\n            me = sess_loader.motion_energy[key]\\n            times = me['times'].to_numpy()\\n            vals = me['whiskerMotionEnergy'].to_numpy()\\n            if len(times) == 0 or np.all(np.isnan(vals)):\\n                continue\\n            out['whisker-motion-energy'] = (times, vals)\\n            camera_used = view\\n            break\\n        except Exception:\\n            continue\\n    if camera_used is None:\\n        raise RuntimeError('no whisker motion energy available')\\n    return out, camera_used\\n\\n\\ndef bin_behaviour_per_trial(target_times, target_vals, align_times):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Resample a behavioural trace onto the 100 trial bins, per trial.\\n\\n    Faithful re-implementation of `ibl_data_utils.get_behavior_per_interval`:\\n      * the trace is sliced to the open interval (t_beg, t_end),\\n      * a trial is rejected when there is no data, when the trace starts more than one bin\\n        after `t_beg` or ends more than one bin before `t_end`, when the interval time is\\n        NaN, or when the slice contains NaNs,\\n      * the remaining trials are linearly interpolated (with linear extrapolation at the\\n        edges) onto `np.linspace(t_beg + binsize, t_end, n_bins)`, i.e. the right edge of\\n        each bin.\\n\\n    The only deviation is that NaNs always reject a trial (the reference's\\n    `allow_nans=False` branch). The reference caching script passes `allow_nans=True` and\\n    lets the model impute NaNs with the trial average at fit time; here the converted\\n    outputs must be valid class labels at every timepoint, and `verify_data_format`\\n    rejects NaNs outright, so NaN-containing trials are dropped instead.\\n\\n    Returns (values (n_trials, NBINS) float64 with NaN rows for rejected trials,\\n             good mask (n_trials,) bool).\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    n = len(align_times)\\n    vals = np.full((n, NBINS), np.nan)\\n    good = np.zeros(n, dtype=bool)\\n\\n    beg = align_times + TIME_WINDOW[0]\\n    end = align_times + TIME_WINDOW[1]\\n    finite = np.isfinite(beg) & np.isfinite(end)\\n    if not np.any(finite):\\n        return vals, good\\n\\n    idx_beg = np.searchsorted(target_times, np.where(finite, beg, np.inf), side='right')\\n    idx_end = np.searchsorted(target_times, np.where(finite, end, np.inf), side='left')\\n\\n    for k in range(n):\\n        if not finite[k]:\\n            continue\\n        tt = target_times[idx_beg[k]:idx_end[k]]\\n        tv = target_vals[idx_beg[k]:idx_end[k]]\\n        if len(tv) == 0:\\n            continue\\n        if np.isnan(tv).any():\\n            continue\\n        if abs(beg[k] - tt[0]) > BINSIZE:      # target data starts too late\\n            continue\\n        if abs(end[k] - tt[-1]) > BINSIZE:     # target data ends too early\\n            continue\\n        x = np.linspace(beg[k] + BINSIZE, end[k], NBINS)\\n        vals[k] = interp1d(tt, tv, kind='linear', fill_value='extrapolate')(x)\\n        good[k] = True\\n    return vals, good\\n\\n\\ndef discretize_tertiles(values):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Discretize a continuous time-varying behaviour into 3 equal-occupancy bins.\\n\\n    Thresholds are the 33.3rd and 66.7th percentiles of every retained (trial, time-bin)\\n    sample of **that session**. Per-session thresholds are used because both signals are in\\n    session-specific units: whisker motion energy is an uncalibrated pixel-intensity\\n    difference whose scale depends on the camera (left 1280x1024 @60 Hz vs right 640x512\\n    @150 Hz), on illumination and on ROI placement, and wheel-speed statistics depend on how\\n    vigorously a given mouse turns the wheel. A single global threshold would map whole\\n    sessions into one class; per-session tertiles give ~1/3 of samples per class in every\\n    session, so chance is a well-defined 1/3 and the shared decoder sees a comparable\\n    target in every session.\\n\\n    Returns (labels (int) in {0,1,2}, thresholds (2,)).\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    finite = values[np.isfinite(values)]\\n    thresholds = np.quantile(finite, [1. / 3., 2. / 3.])\\n    labels = np.searchsorted(thresholds, values, side='right').astype(np.int64)\\n    return labels, thresholds\\n\\n\\ndef trial_number_in_block(probability_left):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"0-based index of each trial within its block of constant `probabilityLeft`.\\n\\n    Computed on the *complete* trials table before any trial is excluded, so that the\\n    numbering reflects the block structure the mouse actually experienced (the IBL task has\\n    an initial 90-trial unbiased block at pLeft = 0.5, then blocks of 20-100 trials\\n    alternating between pLeft = 0.8 and 0.2).\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    p = np.asarray(probability_left, dtype=float)\\n    new_block = np.ones(len(p), dtype=bool)\\n    if len(p) > 1:\\n        # NaN != NaN, so a NaN pLeft always starts a new block; those trials are excluded\\n        # later by the trials mask anyway.\\n        new_block[1:] = ~(p[1:] == p[:-1])\\n    block_id = np.cumsum(new_block) - 1\\n    # index within block = running count restarting at each block boundary\\n    starts = np.nonzero(new_block)[0]\\n    within = np.arange(len(p)) - starts[block_id]\\n    return within.astype(np.float32), block_id\\n\\n\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\n# Per-session conversion\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\ndef convert_session(eid, verbose=True, collect_debug=False):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Convert one session. Returns a dict, or raises on failure.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    timing = {}\\n    one = get_one()\\n    brain_regions = BrainRegions()\\n\\n    t = time.time()\\n    pids, pnames = one.eid2pid(eid)\\n    timing['eid2pid'] = time.time() - t\\n\\n    # ---- neural -----------------------------------------------------------------\\n    t = time.time()\\n    spikes, clusters = load_session_spikes(one, eid, pids, pnames)\\n    timing['load_spikes'] = time.time() - t\\n    n_clusters_all = len(clusters)\\n\\n    t = time.time()\\n    keep_idx, beryl_keep = select_neurons(clusters, brain_regions)\\n    n_neurons = len(keep_idx)\\n    if n_neurons == 0:\\n        raise RuntimeError('no well-isolated grey-matter neurons')\\n    remap = np.full(n_clusters_all, -1, dtype=np.int64)\\n    remap[keep_idx] = np.arange(n_neurons)\\n    sc = remap[spikes['clusters']]\\n    sel = sc >= 0\\n    spike_times = np.ascontiguousarray(spikes['times'][sel])\\n    spike_clusters = np.ascontiguousarray(sc[sel])\\n    timing['select_neurons'] = time.time() - t\\n\\n    # ---- trials -----------------------------------------------------------------\\n    t = time.time()\\n    sess_loader = SessionLoader(one=one, eid=eid)\\n    # `load_trials_and_mask` builds the data paper's trial exclusion mask. Note the\\n    # reference calls `SessionLoader(one, eid)` positionally, which ibllib 4.0.1 no longer\\n    # accepts, hence passing an explicit `sess_loader`.\\n    trials, mask = load_trials_and_mask(\\n        one=one, eid=eid, max_trial_len=MAX_TRIAL_LEN, sess_loader=sess_loader)\\n    mask = np.asarray(mask, dtype=bool)\\n    timing['load_trials'] = time.time() - t\\n    n_trials_all = len(trials)\\n\\n    align_times = trials[ALIGN_TIME].to_numpy()\\n    in_block, _ = trial_number_in_block(trials['probabilityLeft'].to_numpy())\\n\\n    # ---- behaviour --------------------------------------------------------------\\n    t = time.time()\\n    beh_traces, camera_used = load_dynamic_behaviour(sess_loader)\\n    timing['load_behaviour'] = time.time() - t\\n\\n    t = time.time()\\n    wheel_vals, wheel_ok = bin_behaviour_per_trial(*beh_traces['wheel-speed'], align_times)\\n    me_vals, me_ok = bin_behaviour_per_trial(*beh_traces['whisker-motion-energy'], align_times)\\n    timing['bin_behaviour'] = time.time() - t\\n\\n    # ---- trial selection ---------------------------------------------------------\\n    # Mirrors `align_spike_behavior`: keep trials that pass the trials mask AND for which\\n    # every behavioural trace could be extracted.\\n    keep_trials = mask & wheel_ok & me_ok\\n    n_keep = int(keep_trials.sum())\\n    if n_keep < MIN_TRIALS:\\n        raise RuntimeError(f'only {n_keep} usable trials')\\n\\n    # ---- bin spikes (only for the trials we keep) --------------------------------\\n    t = time.time()\\n    binned = bin_spiking_data_fast(spike_times, spike_clusters, n_neurons,\\n                                   align_times[keep_trials])\\n    timing['bin_spikes'] = time.time() - t\\n\\n    # ---- inputs ------------------------------------------------------------------\\n    tr = trials[keep_trials]\\n    inp = np.empty((n_keep, 2, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\\n    inp[:, 0, :] = BIN_CENTRES.astype(np.float32)\\n    inp[:, 1, :] = in_block[keep_trials][:, None]\\n\\n    # ---- outputs -----------------------------------------------------------------\\n    # choice: IBL codes +1 / -1. Verified empirically (see CONVERSION_NOTES Step 4):\\n    # on correct trials with the stimulus on the left, choice == +1; on correct trials with\\n    # the stimulus on the right, choice == -1. So +1 is a leftward choice.\\n    choice = tr['choice'].to_numpy()\\n    choice_out = (choice < 0).astype(np.int64)          # left -> 0, right -> 1\\n\\n    pleft = tr['probabilityLeft'].to_numpy()\\n    prior_out = np.full(n_keep, -1, dtype=np.int64)\\n    for value, code in ((0.2, 0), (0.5, 1), (0.8, 2)):\\n        prior_out[np.isclose(pleft, value)] = code\\n    if np.any(prior_out < 0):\\n        bad = np.unique(pleft[prior_out < 0])\\n        raise RuntimeError(f'unexpected probabilityLeft values {bad}')\\n\\n    wheel_kept = wheel_vals[keep_trials]\\n    me_kept = me_vals[keep_trials]\\n    wheel_lab, wheel_thr = discretize_tertiles(wheel_kept)\\n    me_lab, me_thr = discretize_tertiles(me_kept)\\n\\n    out = np.empty((n_keep, 4, NBINS), dtype=np.int64)\\n    out[:, 0, :] = choice_out[:, None]\\n    out[:, 1, :] = prior_out[:, None]\\n    out[:, 2, :] = wheel_lab\\n    out[:, 3, :] = me_lab\\n\\n    result = dict(\\n        eid=str(eid),\\n        neural=binned,                      # uint8 (n_keep, n_neurons, NBINS)\\n        input=inp,\\n        output=out,\\n        beryl=beryl_keep,\\n        n_clusters_all=int(n_clusters_all),\\n        n_good_all=int((clusters['label'].to_numpy() >= QC_LABEL).sum()),\\n        n_neurons=int(n_neurons),\\n        n_probes=len(pids),\\n        n_trials_all=int(n_trials_all),\\n        n_trials_mask=int(mask.sum()),\\n        n_trials_kept=n_keep,\\n        camera_used=camera_used,\\n        wheel_thresholds=wheel_thr,\\n        me_thresholds=me_thr,\\n        frac_correct=float((trials['feedbackType'].to_numpy() == 1).mean()),\\n        timing=timing,\\n    )\\n    if collect_debug:\\n        result['debug'] = dict(\\n            trials=trials, mask=mask, keep_trials=keep_trials,\\n            align_times=align_times, in_block=in_block,\\n            wheel_trace=beh_traces['wheel-speed'], me_trace=beh_traces['whisker-motion-energy'],\\n            wheel_vals=wheel_kept, me_vals=me_kept,\\n            spike_times=spike_times, spike_clusters=spike_clusters,\\n        )\\n    if verbose:\\n        print(f'  [{eid}] probes={len(pids)} clusters={n_clusters_all} '\\n              f'good={result[\\\"n_good_all\\\"]} kept_neurons={n_neurons} '\\n              f'trials={n_trials_all}->mask {int(mask.sum())}->kept {n_keep} '\\n              f'camera={camera_used} '\\n              f'({sum(timing.values()):.1f}s)', flush=True)\\n    return result\\n\\n\\ndef _worker(eid):\\n    try:\\n        return convert_session(eid, verbose=True)\\n    except Exception as exc:       # noqa: BLE001 -- one bad session must not kill the run\\n        return {'eid': str(eid), 'error': f'{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}',\\n                'traceback': traceback.format_exc()}\\n\\n\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\n# Diagnostic plots\\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\ndef plot_processing(res, outpath):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Plot every processing step for one session, to verify alignment/discretization.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    import matplotlib\\n    matplotlib.use('Agg')\\n    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\\n\\n    dbg = res['debug']\\n    trials, keep = dbg['trials'], dbg['keep_trials']\\n    align = dbg['align_times'][keep]\\n    neural = res['neural'].astype(np.float32)\\n    inp, out = res['input'], res['output']\\n    n_keep = neural.shape[0]\\n    tr_edges = BIN_RIGHT_EDGES\\n    tr_ctr = BIN_CENTRES\\n\\n    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(26, 30))\\n    gs = fig.add_gridspec(7, 3, hspace=0.45, wspace=0.22)\\n\\n    # --- 1. population PSTH: must show a stimulus-locked transient at t = 0 -----------\\n    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :])\\n    psth = neural.mean(axis=(0, 1)) / BINSIZE\\n    ax.plot(tr_ctr, psth, lw=2)\\n    ax.axvline(0, color='r', {ALIGN_TIME} '\\n                 f'({res[\\\"n_neurons\\\"]} neurons, {n_keep} trials)')\\n    ax.legend()\\n\\n    # --- 2. single-trial raster reconstructed from raw spike times vs binned matrix ----\\n    k = min(3, n_keep - 1)\\n    t0 = align[k]\\n    st, sc = dbg['spike_times'], dbg['spike_clusters']\\n    sel = (st >= t0 + TIME_WINDOW[0]) & (st < t0 + TIME_WINDOW[1])\\n    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0])\\n    ax.plot(st[sel] - t0, sc[sel], '|', ms=2, color='k')\\n    ax.axvline(0, color='r', ls='--')\\n    ax.set_xlim(TIME_WINDOW)\\n    ax.set_title(f'raw spike raster, trial {k}')\\n    ax.set_xlabel('time from stim onset (s)'); ax.set_ylabel('neuron')\\n\\n    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1])\\n    ax.imshow(neural[k], aspect='auto', interpolation='nearest', origin='lower',\\n              extent=[TIME_WINDOW[0], TIME_WINDOW[1], 0, res['n_neurons']])\\n    ax.axvline(0, color='r', ls='--')\\n    ax.set_title(f'binned spike counts, trial {k} (20 ms bins)')\\n    ax.set_xlabel('time from stim onset (s)'); ax.set_ylabel('neuron')\\n\\n    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2])\\n    # per-bin totals from the two routes must agree exactly\\n    hist = np.zeros(NBINS)\\n    b = np.floor((st[sel] - (t0 + TIME_WINDOW[0])) / BINSIZE).astype(int)\\n    b = b[(b >= 0) & (b < NBINS)]\\n    np.add.at(hist, b, 1)\\n    ax.step(tr_ctr, hist, where='mid',
